articles.summary: Updates from the series opener at Kingsmead Ground Any thoughts? 42nd over: South Africa 221-5 (Breetzke 86, Jansen 42) Edwards helps bring the run-rate back under control. Australia will take giving up three singles from a tidy over especially with Jansen still swinging wildly.

41st over: South Africa 218-5 (Breetzke 84, Jansen 41) SIX! Jansen goes large and cracks Starc into the back tier of the grandstand. He picks up the slower ball and launches it over deep mid-wicket with a 94 metre hit. The all-rounder finishes the over by picking up the attempted yorker and plundering one of the very best bowlers in the world back over his head to the rope. Australia were in command with South Africa barely more than crawling along but Jansen has quickly turned the game – he has scored 41 in the partnership of 50.

40th over: South Africa 208-5 (Breetzke 84, Jansen 31) Jansen gives himself some room to punch a square drive off Edwards to the rope. The debutant responds with a slower ball that slips out of his hands and down the legside. Edwards limits the damage from there with the South Africans picking up three singles from there.

39th over: South Africa 200-5 (Breetzke 83, Jansen 25) SIX! Jansen is done with hanging around as he picks up the flight from Zampa, takes one step down the pitch and sends the ball sailing over the long-on fence. The towering all-rounder does much the same again as he gets down on one knee and slog sweeps the leg-spinner into the crowd at deep midwicket. That brings up the 200 for South Africa just as they were getting bogged down.

38th over: South Africa 184-5 (Breetzke 82, Jansen 10) Ellis limits South Africa to just the two runs from the over but the batters will need to get motoring soon.

37th over: South Africa 182-5 (Breetzke 81, Jansen 9) Jansen opens up and swings hard at a fuller delivery from Starc. The South Africa all-rounder doesn’t quite connect sweetly but gets enough on it to reach the rope at deep midwicket. Starc almost responds with a delivery that moves away from the off-stump but Jansen isn’t good enough to get even a nick on it.

36th over: South Africa 175-5 (Breetzke 80, Jansen 3) Breetzke gives up a rare half-chance as he pulls Ellis but gets a top edge that flies high to backward square. Inglis races towards the drop but can’t get there in time and Breetzke survives.

35th over: South Africa 171-5 (Breetzke 78, Jansen 1) Starc returns with Australia hoping to take another wicket with Jansen fresh at the crease. Breetzke has no concern turning the strike over to the all-rounder with a single to mid-off, and Jansen adds another with a flick off the pads. Breetzke picks up one more to mid-wicket.

34th over: South Africa 168-5 (Breetzke 76, Jansen 0) Ellis picks up a wicket with his wicked variation leaving Miller all at sea. He took a quality reflex catch to send Miller on his way.

Nathan Ellis returns and jumps straight into a pair of slower balls. David Miller has to check each of his shots but looks in little danger. But he fails to adjust in time to a straighter delivery as he spoons the ball back to the bowler and Ellis clings on to the catch while barely out of his delivery stride.

33rd over: South Africa 166-4 (Breetzke 75, Miller 10) Hazlewood is the next to strike Breetzke in the stomach. That’s the second big blow the South African has taken in the space of a few overs and he takes a hard earned breather.

32nd over: South Africa 165-4 (Breetzke 75, Miller 9) Breetzke takes to Edwards now as he gets on the front foot and punishes an overpitched delivery straight down the ground for four. Edwards gets one to nip back in and while he can’t take the crucial wicket he lands a nasty blow on Breetzke’s midriff.

31st over: South Africa 159-4 (Breetzke 70, Miller 8) Hazlewood takes the ball as Australia search for a wicket after the drinks break. Breetzke takes a few deliveries to pick up the line and length then launches a huge SIX over deep square leg. Hazlewood was barely short but Breetzke is in red-hot form.

30th over: South Africa 152-4 (Breetzke 63, Miller 8) Edwards keeps the pressure on with another tidy over as the batting pair pick up three singles. That’s drinks with this ODI evenly poised.

29th over: South Africa 149-4 (Breetzke 61, Miller 7) Breetzke gets down on one knee and smacks a drive through cover to the rope. He goes back-to-back with a pull off Zampa to deep mid-wicket where Starc dives to collect the ball but his foot crashes over the padding.

28th over: South Africa 138-4 (Breetzke 50, Miller 7) Jack Edwards gets the ball to jag back into the left-hander David Miller and it crashes into the South African’s back pad. The umpire waves away the appeal and Australia send it for a review. The only thing saving Miller – and denying Edwards a first ODI wickets – is umpire’s call as ball tracking shows it was clipping the bails. Miller survives again as a thick leading edge flies over cover but lands safely and the South African scamper through for a couple.

27th over: South Africa 134-4 (Breetzke 50, Miller 5) Millers gets off the mark with a flick off the pads to deep long-on and picks up two more behind square off Zampa.

26th over: South Africa 129-4 (Breetzke 50, Miller 0) Half-century for Breetzke. That’s the eighth time he has reached the mark in 14 ODIs. He brings it up with a cracking straight drive to the rope off Renshaw. The Australian part-timer ties him down to see out the rest of the over.

25th over: South Africa 125-4 (Breetzke 46, Miller 0) Rickelton was looking dangerous while scoring at a touch better than a run a ball but is on his way for 27 off 26. David Miller joins Breetzke at the crease as South Africa will appreciate having a bit of depth to their batting order.

Rickelton takes on Renshaw on the rope at deep square and falls narrowly short of clearing the Australian. It is a tricky catch with Renshaw close to the boundary and perhaps receiving some live feedback from the crowd. He skips up on to one leg, clasps the catch, turns to the crowd and beams without needing to say a word. It was an ordinary ball from Zampa, far too short, but Rickelton paid for mistiming the stroke.

24th over: South Africa 123-3 (Breetzke 45, Rickelton 26) Edwards returns and Rickelton almost gives the all-rounder his first ODI wicket. Rickelton drives and gets a thick edge that flies wide of the keeper and past deep third to the rope. The next boundary is pure class as Rickelton cracks a straight drive wide of mid-off.

23rd over: South Africa 112-3 (Breetzke 44, Rickelton 16) Rickelton hammers Starc for back-to-back boundaries even as the left-armer is pushing into mid 140km/h deliveries. The first uses the pace to ease the ball through deep square and fine leg. The next is more impressive as Rickelton rocks back and cuts through point to the rope.

22nd over: South Africa 103-3 (Breetzke 44, Rickelton 7) Australia roll the dice with the part-time spin of Matt Renshaw and might be pleased to get away with just the one boundary. Rickelton misses out on full toss as he hits straight to long-off. Breetzke likes what he’s seen and immediately takes on Renshaw with a scorching cover drive to the rope.

21st over: South Africa 96-3 (Breetzke 39, Rickelton 5) Starc returns with Australia looking to turn the screw before Rickelton settles. The left-armer immediately gets movement in the air when others were unable to find much. Three singles keep the score ticking over as Connolly saves a boundary with a dive in cover off the last ball of the over.

20th over: South Africa 93-3 (Breetzke 38, Rickelton 3) Ellis reins in the scoring with an over filled with his usual variation. Full, short, wide of off-stump and a slower ball keep the batters guessing. Breetzke picks up a single to deep square and Rickelton adds another to mid-off.

19th over: South Africa 90-3 (Breetzke 37, Rickelton 1) Zampa sends Bavuma on his way to bring Ryan Rickelton to the crease at No 5 – the lowest the hard-hitter has batted in his 17 ODIs. Rickelton gets off the mark with a single to mid-off then Breetzke cracks a SIX as he sends a shorter ball over deep mid-wicket.

Adam Zampa with the timely breakthrough as Temba Bavuma gifts his wicket to the Australians. The leg-spinner throws up a tempting delivery that is very wide of the off-stump and the South African skipper can’t resist swiping hard but gets an edge through to the keeper. A nice take from Inglis too.

18th over: South Africa 83-2 (Bavuma 30, Breetzke 31) The South Africans share a 50-run partnership as Breetzke opens up his bat to slice a drive off Ellis past point and to the rope. Fortune perhaps favouring the brave but the batters are looking solid.

17th over: South Africa 76-2 (Bavuma 29, Breetzke 25) The South Africa pair are looking settled and are closing in on a 50-run stand. Breetzke hammers a fuller ball from Zampa as a cover drive ends up flying over point to the rope.

16th over: South Africa 70-2 (Bavuma 28, Breetzke 20) Cooper Connolly comes into the attack as Australia call on spin and both ends. He begins around the wicket and Breetzke picks off a single to long-off. Bavuma has a closer look then flicks off his pads for two to long-on as Breetzke races through for a tight second that tests Travis Head’s throw from the deep. Bavuma punishes a shorter ball with a cut to the rope.

15th over: South Africa 63-2 (Bavuma 22, Breetzke 19) Australia turn to spin after the drinks break with Adam Zampa thrown the ball for the first time. The South Africans begin the over with three consecutive singles before the leg-spinner clamps down.

14th over: South Africa 60-2 (Bavuma 21, Breetzke 17) Bavuma flicks a switch with a pair of sublime boundaries. The first comes off the back foot as the skipper crunches a straight drive over Edwards’ head. The next is even better with a textbook pull shot over square leg. That’s drinks.

13th over: South Africa 52-2 (Bavuma 13, Breetzke 17) Hazlewood bowls his sixth over of the spell. Breetzke crunches a boundary with an exquisite straight drive that thunders just wide of mid-off.

12th over: South Africa 46-2 (Bavuma 12, Breetzke 12) Jack Edwards is thrown the ball for the first time in an ODI. A neat over only gives up two runs as Bavuma starts it with a nudge to square leg and Breetzke ends it with a risky single to mid-on.

11th over: South Africa 44-2 (Bavuma 11, Breetzke 11) South Africa are happy to consolidate on their decent start by rotating the strike with four singles off Hazlewood. The Australian quick drops in a nasty bouncer to Bavuma as the South Africa tries to hook. There is a half-hearted appeal for caught behind but Bavuma was nowhere near it.

10th over: South Africa 40-2 (Bavuma 9, Breetzke 9) A tidy over from Ellis. Bavuma picks up a single with a cover drive that doesn’t have enough on it to beat the infield. Breetzke adds one with a straight drive and a tight run. Powerplay is done. Honours feel even.

9th over: South Africa 38-2 (Bavuma 8, Breetzke 8) Hazlewood continues but the South Africans are beginning to look more comfortable against him. Bavuma picks up a single with a nudge around the corner to midwicket. Breetzke then opens up with a square cut off the back foot for four. Shot of the day so far.

8th over: South Africa 33-2 (Bavuma 7, Breetzke 4) Ellis gets the crucial wicket of De Kock to bring South Africa one-day wonder Matthew Breetzke to the crease. The 27-year-old averages 59.17 with one ton and six half-centuries from his first 13 innings in the format. Ellis beats Breetzke with the first ball. But the South African responds with a straight drive past the bowler and to the rope off the final delivery of the over.

Nathan Ellis comes into the attack and strikes first ball. It was no loosener as he angles the ball across Quinton de Kock and forces the opener into playing a half-hearted defensive stroke. The ball clips the shoulder of the bat and Inglis dives hard across Renshaw at first slip to claim a nice catch.

7th over: South Africa 29-1 (De Kock 14, Bavuma 7) South Africa get motoring helped by a rare loose over from Starc. The left-arm quick drifts down leg for a wide then loses both his line and length with a stray delivery down the same side. Inglis can’t get to it and the ball races away for five wides.

6th over: South Africa 21-1 (De Kock 13, Bavuma 6) SIX! Quinton de Kock launches a pull shot beyond the rope for the first six of the innings. Hazlewood is only a little short of his spot but the opener has enough time to lean back and pull over square and clear of Adam Zampa on the boundary.

5th over: South Africa 14-1 (De Kock 7, Bavuma 5) Bavuma gets South Africa moving a touch as he punishes a fuller delivery from Mitchell Starc. The cover drive was in the air a touch longer than he would have liked but it lands safely on the way to the rope. The skipper ends the over trying to flick the left-armer off his pads but can only pick up one leg-bye.

4th over: South Africa 9-1 (De Kock 7, Bavuma 1) Hazlewood gets the breakthrough with the wicket of Tony de Zorzi and almost has a second with a big lbw shout against Temba Bavuma. The South Africa skipper is given the benefit of the doubt as he defends a straight one. Australia send the decision for a review that shows the ball strikes Bavuma on the back pad, hits him dead in front of the stumps … but is bouncing over.

The South Africa left-hander found Hazlewood hard to get away earlier and when finally given a hint of room he can’t help but open up. The Australia quick drifts a touch wider of the off-stump with the ball moving away and De Zorzi drives hard but can only get an edge to Matt Renshaw at first slip.

3rd over: South Africa 6-0 (De Kock 6, De Zorzi 0) Quinton de Kock plays with a watchful eye as Starc works away outside his off-stump. The left-handed opener finally pounces on a shorter delivery to lift the ball over a vacant gully area to the rope wide of deep third.

2nd over: South Africa 2-0 (De Kock 2, De Zorzi 0) Josh Hazlewood takes the new ball from the other end as is immediately on to his metronomic line and length. Tony de Zorzi defends soundly to see out a maiden.

1st over: South Africa 2-0 (De Kock 2, De Zorzi 0) Mitchell Starc gets the ball talking from the opening delivery as it swings away from left-hander Quinton de Kock. The Australian quick drifts on to the pads with a straighter ball that De Kock whips away for an easy two. De Kock ends the over punching a drive straight down the ground as Starc gets a finger on the ball on its way through to the stumps. Tony de Zorzi is awake to the danger and has his bat grounded.

Quinton de Kock and Tony de Zorzi make their way to the crease for South Africa with the national anthems sung and done. Australia have a formidable pace attack to turn to with Mitchell Starc taking the new ball and Josh Hazlewood also named alongside the variation of Nathan Ellis and debutant Jack Edwards.

South Africa: Quinton de Kock (wk), Tony de Zorzi, Temba Bavuma (capt), Matthew Breetzke, Ryan Rickelton, David Miller, Marco Jansen, Corbin Bosch, Gerald Coetzee, Bjorn Fortuin, Keshav Maharaj.

South Africa will rely on spin rather than pace as their depth is tested due to injuries. The absence of Aiden Markram is a big blow with the powerhouse batter missing for personal reasons, while Dewald Brevis and Tristan Stubbs have been left out.

Australia: Travis Head, Mitchell Marsh (capt), Cooper Connolly, Josh Inglis (wk), Matt Renshaw, Cameron Green, Jack Edwards, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Ellis, Adam Zampa, Josh Hazlewood.

The tourists turn to pace with Jack Edwards handed an ODI debut. The big name pushed out is Alex Carey with Josh Inglis to take the gloves. Batting prodigy Ollie Peake is also absent after showing some decent form in Zimbabwe, while Cameron Green is back in the XI though it remains to be seen if the all-rounder bowls as well as bats.

Australia win the toss and elect to bowl . Captain Mitch Marsh talks up the early start with first ball coming at 10am local time in Durban with a breeze blowing across Kingsmead Ground and expected to generate some movement in the air.

Hello and welcome to live coverage of the first one-day international between South Africa and Australia in Durban. This the first of three ODIs between the old foes as they take tentative steps down a long path towards the Cricket World Cup to be jointly hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Namibia in little more than 12 months’ time.

But as much as the attention is now on a rare 50-over series in South Africa, and further ahead to the celebration of cricket that is expected for the continent next year, there is no denying the Test series that waits just around the corner is as much front of mind for both sides as well as their fans.

Australia usually time their run to hit top white-ball form for World Cup stages but started to tune up when sweeping a three-match ODI series in Zimbabwe. But South Africa have had a stranglehold on ODI series against their rivals, winning the past five at home and away going back a decade to September 2016. That includes when Australia and South Africa last played an ODI series just over a year ago when the tourists won the opening two games in Cairns and Mackay. Australia claimed a consolation win when scoring 431-2 – their second-highest ODI total, behind their 434-4 against South Africa in that remarkable game 19 years ago. We can only dream of similar fireworks in Durban today.

Toss and confirmed teams will be coming up shortly – with the first ball to be bowled at 10am in Durban / 6pm AEST – so you have time to get in touch with your thoughts and predictions. Drop me an email or find me @martinpegan on Bluesky or X .

The left-arm quick drifts down leg for a wide then loses both his line and length with a stray delivery down the same side. Inglis can’t get to it and the ball races away for five wides.

6th over: South Africa 21-1 (De Kock 13, Bavuma 6) SIX! Quinton de Kock launches a pull shot beyond the rope for the first six of the innings. Hazlewood is only a little short of his spot but the opener has enough time to lean back and pull over square and clear of Adam Zampa on the boundary.

5th over: South Africa 14-1 (De Kock 7, Bavuma 5) Bavuma gets South Africa moving a touch as he punishes a fuller delivery from Mitchell Starc. The cover drive was in the air a touch longer than he would have liked but it lands safely on the way to the rope. The skipper ends the over trying to flick the left-armer off his pads but can only pick up one leg-bye.

4th over: South Africa 9-1 (De Kock 7, Bavuma 1) Hazlewood gets the breakthrough with the wicket of Tony de Zorzi and almost has a second with a big lbw shout against Temba Bavuma. The South Africa skipper is given the benefit of the doubt as he defends a straight one. Australia send the decision for a review that shows the ball strikes Bavuma on the back pad, hits him dead in front of the stumps … but is bouncing over.

The South Africa left-hander found Hazlewood hard to get away earlier and when finally given a hint of room he can’t help but open up. The Australia quick drifts a touch wider of the off-stump with the ball moving away and De Zorzi drives hard but can only get an edge to Matt Renshaw at first slip.

3rd over: South Africa 6-0 (De Kock 6, De Zorzi 0) Quinton de Kock plays with a watchful eye as Starc works away outside his off-stump. The left-handed opener finally pounces on a shorter delivery to lift the ball over a vacant gully area to the rope wide of deep third.

2nd over: South Africa 2-0 (De Kock 2, De Zorzi 0) Josh Hazlewood takes the new ball from the other end as is immediately on to his metronomic line and length. Tony de Zorzi defends soundly to see out a maiden.

1st over: South Africa 2-0 (De Kock 2, De Zorzi 0) Mitchell Starc gets the ball talking from the opening delivery as it swings away from left-hander Quinton de Kock. The Australian quick drifts on to the pads with a straighter ball that De Kock whips away for an easy two. De Kock ends the over punching a drive straight down the ground as Starc gets a finger on the ball on its way through to the stumps. Tony de Zorzi is awake to the danger and has his bat grounded.

Quinton de Kock and Tony de Zorzi make their way to the crease for South Africa with the national anthems sung and done. Australia have a formidable pace attack to turn to with Mitchell Starc taking the new ball and Josh Hazlewood also named alongside the variation of Nathan Ellis and debutant Jack Edwards.
South Africa: Quinton de Kock (wk), Tony de Zorzi, Temba Bavuma (capt), Matthew Breetzke, Ryan Rickelton, David Miller, Marco Jansen, Corbin Bosch, Gerald Coetzee, Bjorn Fortuin, Keshav Maharaj.

South Africa will rely on spin rather than pace as their depth is tested due to injuries. The absence of Aiden Markram is a big blow with the powerhouse batter missing for personal reasons, while Dewald Brevis and Tristan Stubbs have been left out.
Australia: Travis Head, Mitchell Marsh (capt), Cooper Connolly, Josh Inglis (wk), Matt Renshaw, Cameron Green, Jack Edwards, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Ellis, Adam Zampa, Josh Hazlewood.

The tourists turn to pace with Jack Edwards handed an ODI debut. The big name pushed out is Alex Carey with Josh Inglis to take the gloves. Batting prodigy Ollie Peake is also absent after showing some decent form in Zimbabwe, while Cameron Green is back in the XI though it remains to be seen if the all-rounder bowls as well as bats.

Australia win the toss and elect to bowl . Captain Mitch Marsh talks up the early start with first ball coming at 10am local time in Durban with a breeze blowing across Kingsmead Ground and expected to generate some movement in the air.

Hello and welcome to live coverage of the first one-day international between South Africa and Australia in Durban. This the first of three ODIs between the old foes as they take tentative steps down a long path towards the Cricket World Cup to be jointly hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Namibia in little more than 12 months’ time.

But as much as the attention is now on a rare 50-over series in South Africa, and further ahead to the celebration of cricket that is expected for the continent next year, there is no denying the Test series that waits just around the corner is as much front of mind for both sides as well as their fans.

Australia usually time their run to hit top white-ball form for World Cup stages but started to tune up when sweeping a three-match ODI series in Zimbabwe. But South Africa have had a stranglehold on ODI series against their rivals, winning the past five at home and away going back a decade to September 2016. That includes when Australia and South Africa last played an ODI series just over a year ago when the tourists won the opening two games in Cairns and Mackay. Australia claimed a consolation win when scoring 431-2 – their second-highest ODI total, behind their 434-4 against South Africa in that remarkable game 19 years ago. We can only dream of similar fireworks in Durban today.

Toss and confirmed teams will be coming up shortly – with the first ball to be bowled at 10am in Durban / 6pm AEST – so you have time to get in touch with your thoughts and predictions. Drop me an email or find me @martinpegan on Bluesky or X .

articles.content:
Notts have lost their first at Trent Bridge, Ben Slater edging a rising ball from Ben Coad to Adam Lyth at slip. Notts 59-1.

At Old Trafford, Ben McKinney has gone to fifty off 74 balls for Durham but – don’t tell Big Kookaburra’s Gary Naylor – it’s the fourth Dukes ball of the morning they have gone through in the opening twenty or so overs. That’s a bad batch. Durham 112-1

“Radical thought… too much turns on the toss in late September, as scorecards today attest. At Lord’s, the ball isn’t hooping or seaming miles, but it’s doing enough for Northants’ batters to push hard at it with a “get some runs now because there’s one with your name on it” attitude. What is to be done?

Well, why not play this last tranche of Championship fixtures with the much maligned old Kookaburra? That might tip the balance back towards the batting side and make 10.30am starts more even.”

I take your point Gary, I do, but also if it was so cut and dried I am confused as to why some teams, including Leicestershire here at Edgbaston who are 63-5, would choose to bat first? Herein lies the wonder of cricket and the unreadable nature of pitches, balls and conditions?

I’ll do a lunchtime sweep around the grounds but am currently all eyes on the action here at Edgbaston with Leicestershire 55-5, Ben Cox and Ian Holland digging in against Hannon-Dalby and Barnard. There’s a sense that a wicket could fall almost every ball.

Ollie Hannon-Dalby strikes here at Edgbaston! Leicestershire are now 47-4 and in some serious trouble… make that 47-5! Sol Budinger nicks off to Ed Barnard and is snaffled by the teflon handed Rob Yates at second slip. Carnage.

No sooner had I pressed send on Luke’s morning dispatch than the alert pings that Vasconcelos has nicked off to second slip to leave Northants 46-5! Gulp.

M’esteemed colleague Luke McLaughlin is at Lord’s and sends this missive after the first hour of play. Northants are in big trouble already:

Sunshine has broken out at Lord’s after a cloudy start, where it feels more late August than late September, and the pavilion is well populated. The climate is changing but Toby Roland-Jones remains constant, the 38-year-old dealing an early blow to Northamptonshire’s promotion hopes by removing Luke Proctor lbw for 0 in the first over. Gus Miller went for 10, also lbw to Ryan Higgins, and Saif Zaib was caught at first slip off the same bowler, before Calvin Harrison slapped a Danru Ferns long-hop to cover. No 1 batter Ricardo Vasconcelos survived a confident caught-behind appeal off Higgins in the fourth over, but has looked solid for 26 not out, and has left the ball well. Not the start the visitors wanted after winning the toss and batting, though: 44-4 off 14 overs .”

That man Jack Leach has got the breakthrough in Taunton. Michael Vaughan and Steve Finn have both been calling for Leach to be recalled into the Test side, definitely one to keep an eye on, particularly with the Bangladesh series early next year.

Leach snares his old England teammate Rory Burns who plays a loose sweep and gifts a top edge to Tom Abell.

I’ve arrived at Edgbaston to see Ethan Bamber deliver his seventh over on the spin with sun bursting through the clouds. Leicestershire need it to flatten this pitch into the roadiest road pronto… Baby faced assassin Bamber has 1-13 and Woakes 2-11. Tidy.

A ripple of applause for the introduction of Ollie Hannon-Dalby. I enjoyed his chat with Tanya ahead of this game:

His long career gives him the perspective to see how the game has been transformed, and what matters. “Cricket has changed a little bit, there are lots of offshoots, and the franchise world of course. But on a day-to-day basis, the measure of you as a cricketer is either Test cricket if you can play it, or otherwise the County Championship.

To do well in county cricket is incredibly satisfying, and being able to win the championship is a great marker in your career. It says a lot that the great Chris Woakes could have sailed off into the sunset, but he has stayed for weeks like this.” By Sunday, we will know how the die fell.”

“Off-topic: Mark Wood is one of only two cricketers in my short time following the sport who I’ve thought, “There’s a cricketer I’d love to sit down and have a chat with.” (Moeen Ali the other.) This is partly due to me not knowing much about most cricketers, but Mark Wood was so odd, so interesting that he broke through that barrier. Seemed like a genuinely lovely chap who kept his weird personality despite his time in the limelight. Amazing cricketer as well.

First-class and Test cricket has lost a goodun, but it’s the commentary box’s gain. Every radio and TV platform showing the cricket should be showering him with offers.”

Toby Roland Jones has picked up an early wicket at Lord’s, Procter pinned LBW…

It’s all go at Edgbaston, the Wizard Woakes nips one back into Rishi Patel who offers no shot and is stone dead. There are good leaves and bad leaves, son … Leics 10-2 and in the mire after choosing to bat.

Ethan Bamber bowls Sheridan Gumbs with the fourth ball of the day at Edgbaston! It’s a beauty that nips in a touch and beats the outside edge of Gumbs’ textbook forward defence to kiss the off bail! Bamber hares off in delight!

DingDingDingDing! For one last time this ‘summer’ whites clad county players take to the field. Let’s play!

Good news! The weather is set fair around the country with only a small chance of rain coming in a bit later on and only in a few places. That’s a very detailed forecast eh? Schafernaker is safe for now…

Warwickshire have their destiny in their own hands, 14 points will see them crowned Division One Champs. They don’t even have to win outright either, a draw with six bonus points gets the job done.

Somerset are 11 points behind in second place and last year’s winners Nottinghamshire 15 behind.

Hampshire are down already, Leicestershire (who are due to appeal their 27 point pitch infraction deduction, say that ten times fast ) and Essex are battling to not be the other team relegated to Div 2.

Leics have to beat Warwickshire and scoop some bonus points to realistically have any chance of dropping down and Essex need to not lose to Glammy. It’s all much more complicated than that of course but you don’t need me to tell you that.

Lord’s : Middlesex v Northamptonshire – Northants win the toss and bat

Hello and welcome to the final round of the 2026 County Championship .

Jim here, I’m stepping into Tanya’s red stillettos, yes they have a prominent Dukes seam circling around the toe , for the next two days. Be gentle won’t you?

I’m currently on the rattler up to Edgbaston to see if Warwickshire can get the job done against Leicestershire. A fair few folk in Somerset will be hoping the next few days take a different course.

That’s just at the top of Division One. We’ll have an eye on all of the action across the shires and the comments below the line will be open for your musings, frustrations and exultations.

Join us for all the end of season stories as they unfold. Play starts around the grounds at 10:30am. All aboard!

articles.title: England v Sri Lanka: second men’s one-day cricket international – live
articles.summary: Over-by-over updates, second ODI from 12.30pm BST Twenty-five ways cricket has changed since 2000 Jofra Archer has the new ball in hand ; Pathum Nissanka is waiting to face him. Let’s play darts. “Nooooo!” Continue reading...
articles.content:
Jofra Archer has the new ball in hand ; Pathum Nissanka is waiting to face him. Let’s play darts.

There was something about Dan Lawrence’s pained groan at Edgbaston in England’s first innings of the third Test against Pakistan. For a split second it looked as if he might plunge his bat into the turf like some tormented Norse warrior. His stumps had already been flattened by his own hand, an attempt to run the ball down past point off Mohammad Imran had ended in him hacking an innocuous delivery emphatically on to them.

The stump microphone amplified Lawrence’s anguished reaction, the noise emanating from his mouth oscillating somewhere between the visceral howl of treading on an upturned plug and the disappointed yelp of missing the last train home. He had been bowled for 65 and another chance of a first Test century had gone begging.

Test batters will tell you how they didn’t feel they “belonged” until they had made a century. That the longer they had to wait to cross the Rubicon of three figures the more it weighed them down. Lawrence has played 17 Tests for England since his first call-up in 2021. It has been a career of fits and starts through no fault of his own; in the past five years he has batted at Nos 7, 6, 5, 4 and 3 as well as a doomed stint as a makeshift opener. It’s those starts that will eat away at him, though.

South Africa’s Matthew Breetzke has continued the spectacular start to his ODI career. He’s currently 84 not out against Australia in Durban; you can follow that game with Martin Pegan and Geoff Lemon.

To reach for the career stats on Cricinfo is no way to go about it. This is a full-on YouTube job: boil the kettle, load up those spells at Headingley, St Lucia and the rest, and take in the whippy, absurd, mesmerising sight of perhaps the fastest English bowler there has ever been. That’s probably the best way to remember Mark Wood’s career.

Tuesday’s announcement of his international retirement was coming from the moment Wood hobbled out of the Ashes last December, the series opener his only appearance. That always felt like the last act, one he rushed back for after surgery on his left knee earlier that year, and the game moves on fast. England’s seam stocks look healthy across formats, with Jofra Archer there to ramp it up when required. It’s a sore point that Archer and Wood played just two Tests together: one without supporters during the 2020 Covid-bubble summer, the other Wood’s farewell at Perth.

The 36-year-old leaves with 119 Test wickets at 30.8 and 80 one-day international wickets at 40.8, figures that need dissecting. He sparkled when it mattered in 50-over cricket, taking 18 wickets in the 2019 World Cup triumph , and there is a clear before-and-after with the red ball. Having made his debut in 2015, it took nearly four years for it all to click together, only after Wood lengthened his run-up and was told by Trevor Bayliss that he wanted to see a bit more “mongrel” from his quick.

Wood responded by clocking 95mph on the way to his first Test five-wicket haul, against West Indies in February 2019 at the age of 29, setting up his own Benjamin Button tale. From that Test in St Lucia, his 13th, until his last, he averaged 27, all while hurling the ball with a lithe frame at obscene, unhealthy speeds.

England are unchanged. Sri Lanka bring in Eshan Malinga for Dushmantha Chameera.

England Banton, Duckett, Root, Brook (c), Buttler (wk), Jacks, Rehan, Overton, Atkinson, Archer, Tongue.

Sri Lanka Nissanka, Kamindu Mendis, Kusal Mendis (c/wk), Rathnayeke, Asalanka, Liyanage, Wellalage, Colombage, Malinga, Fernando, Madushanka.

It’s a lovely autumnal day at Headingley. “Looks like a really good wicket,” says Kusal Mendis. “We have to put a score on the board.”

There’s an orgy of live cricket at Guardian Unlimited today . As well as this game, we have:

Harry Brook had called on his ­England players to continue the “high-octane” cricket witnessed during their clean sweep in the Twenty20s but this latest victory over Sri Lanka in the first one-day international was more of a slow-burn affair.

Gone was the neck-arching carnage of the previous week and in its place, on a tired end-of-season surface, England were bowled out for 265 in 48.1 overs. Brook top-scored with 67 under a warm September sun, before his bowlers rolled the tourists for 176 to take a 1-0 lead into Thursday’s second match at Headingley.

Familiarity with conditions doubtless played its part and Sri Lanka, on the wrong side of the toss, never truly felt in the hunt. For Brook it was an 11th victory as England’s ODI captain, nudging him into credit after 10 defeats and continuing what has been a quiet resurgence in the format this year.

It’s been a while*, you know. Since England won three ODI series in a row; it’s been a while. The last time it happened was in 2023, just before the World Cup, when everything was going to be alright on the night.

That grisly title defence was the start of a desperate few years in ODI cricket, but there are signs that Brendon McCullum is giving England the kiss of life in a third format. If they beat Sri Lanka at Headingley today – and it’ll be an eye-widener if they don’t – England will complete a third series victory of 2026.

At this stage they are no more than dangerous outsiders for next year’s World Cup, but even that would have been unimaginable during the annus horribilis of 2025. England lost 11 out of 15 ODIs and their captain was almost ironed out by a bouncer the night before a game. Off and especially on the field, it feels like a long time ago.

* If these four words made your brain jump straight to a Linoleum song, you win an ephemeral trip back to 1997.

This is a full-on YouTube job: boil the kettle, load up those spells at Headingley, St Lucia and the rest, and take in the whippy, absurd, mesmerising sight of perhaps the fastest English bowler there has ever been. That’s probably the best way to remember Mark Wood’s career.

Tuesday’s announcement of his international retirement was coming from the moment Wood hobbled out of the Ashes last December, the series opener his only appearance. That always felt like the last act, one he rushed back for after surgery on his left knee earlier that year, and the game moves on fast. England’s seam stocks look healthy across formats, with Jofra Archer there to ramp it up when required. It’s a sore point that Archer and Wood played just two Tests together: one without supporters during the 2020 Covid-bubble summer, the other Wood’s farewell at Perth.

The 36-year-old leaves with 119 Test wickets at 30.8 and 80 one-day international wickets at 40.8, figures that need dissecting. He sparkled when it mattered in 50-over cricket, taking 18 wickets in the 2019 World Cup triumph , and there is a clear before-and-after with the red ball. Having made his debut in 2015, it took nearly four years for it all to click together, only after Wood lengthened his run-up and was told by Trevor Bayliss that he wanted to see a bit more “mongrel” from his quick.

Wood responded by clocking 95mph on the way to his first Test five-wicket haul, against West Indies in February 2019 at the age of 29, setting up his own Benjamin Button tale. From that Test in St Lucia, his 13th, until his last, he averaged 27, all while hurling the ball with a lithe frame at obscene, unhealthy speeds.
England are unchanged. Sri Lanka bring in Eshan Malinga for Dushmantha Chameera.
England Banton, Duckett, Root, Brook (c), Buttler (wk), Jacks, Rehan, Overton, Atkinson, Archer, Tongue.
Sri Lanka Nissanka, Kamindu Mendis, Kusal Mendis (c/wk), Rathnayeke, Asalanka, Liyanage, Wellalage, Colombage, Malinga, Fernando, Madushanka.
It’s a lovely autumnal day at Headingley. “Looks like a really good wicket,” says Kusal Mendis. “We have to put a score on the board.”
There’s an orgy of live cricket at Guardian Unlimited today . As well as this game, we have:

Harry Brook had called on his ­England players to continue the “high-octane” cricket witnessed during their clean sweep in the Twenty20s but this latest victory over Sri Lanka in the first one-day international was more of a slow-burn affair.

Gone was the neck-arching carnage of the previous week and in its place, on a tired end-of-season surface, England were bowled out for 265 in 48.1 overs. Brook top-scored with 67 under a warm September sun, before his bowlers rolled the tourists for 176 to take a 1-0 lead into Thursday’s second match at Headingley.

Familiarity with conditions doubtless played its part and Sri Lanka, on the wrong side of the toss, never truly felt in the hunt. For Brook it was an 11th victory as England’s ODI captain, nudging him into credit after 10 defeats and continuing what has been a quiet resurgence in the format this year.

It’s been a while*, you know. Since England won three ODI series in a row; it’s been a while. The last time it happened was in 2023, just before the World Cup, when everything was going to be alright on the night.

That grisly title defence was the start of a desperate few years in ODI cricket, but there are signs that Brendon McCullum is giving England the kiss of life in a third format. If they beat Sri Lanka at Headingley today – and it’ll be an eye-widener if they don’t – England will complete a third series victory of 2026.

At this stage they are no more than dangerous outsiders for next year’s World Cup, but even that would have been unimaginable during the annus horribilis of 2025. England lost 11 out of 15 ODIs and their captain was almost ironed out by a bouncer the night before a game. Off and especially on the field, it feels like a long time ago.
* If these four words made your brain jump straight to a Linoleum song, you win an ephemeral trip back to 1997.

articles.title: Are we back in big tech's 'move fast and break things' era?
articles.summary: Despite promises to make safe AI, examples of bots behaving badly are now coming at us thick and fast.
articles.content:
Watch: What you need to know about the OpenAI Australian government hack

It was a mantra coined by the tech giant Meta and used until 2012, which came to define the bad old days of social media running riot in a feeding frenzy of user data.

Yet now we have large companies scrambling to develop ever more powerful AI, in an intense global race to be first to build the world's most advanced models, egged on by US President Donald Trump.

Despite numerous pledges, commitments and open letters over the years from the industry, promising to prioritise safe, responsible AI aligned with human values, examples of bots behaving badly – to put it mildly - are now coming at us thick and fast.

OpenAI's agents seem to feature quite prominently in the current roll call of AI products taking their remits to extremes.

The Australian government is fuming at the firm's most recent disclosure, that its products accessed both public and non-public data from part of the country's online Medicare healthcare system.

It happened in June, but OpenAI didn't notice until August. It notified the authorities in September.

As Camilla Chan, founder of the cyber-security firm X-Phy, puts it: "The future of autonomous AI cannot rest on companies discovering their own failures and reporting it afterwards."

Protests calling for an end to the "AI race" in Silicon Valley and beyond have intensified in recent months

Worse still, the agents were reportedly able to plot the attack using a German web forum they secretly took over in June, according to ABC's Cam Wilson , external .

When the website's editors noticed and started deleting pages, the agents shared code designed to retrieve them .

And that happened before the Hugging Face incident, described at the time as the world's first AI-enabled cyber-attack.

It raises a question - if the Medicare incident had been carried out by a person rather than an AI agent, would they be in big trouble?

"If this was an individual hacking Australia's Medicare system, they'd be looking at jail time," said Dr Andrew Rogoyski from the Institute for People-Centred AI at the University of Surrey.

"The fact that it's an AI seems to allow the company to shrug their shoulders and get away with 'accidents happen'."

Australia says it is carrying out an urgent review into whether any laws have been broken, but part of that rests on being able to prove intent – which OpenAI denies.

And its government may have to ask itself some awkward questions about the strength of its cyber-security defences, including whether the healthcare data could have been better protected.

Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?

The industry has warned countries and institutions to prepare for a new world of supersized cyber-attacks powered by AI.

A popular solution to keeping the tech on the straight and narrow lies in two parts: slowing down the pace of its development, and implementing international regulation to police it.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham highlighted the need for new global AI standards in his first international speech at the UN General Assembly .

And last night both Sam Altman from OpenAI and Dario Amodei from Anthropic addressed the UN Security Council and pleaded for both – despite US President Donald Trump not being at all enthusiastic about this approach.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!" he posted on Truth Social earlier this month .

Although he has since said he intends to appoint an AI tsar, so perhaps somebody has had a quiet word.

Yesterday I spoke with a senior executive at the top of one of the US's biggest AI firms, and I asked him what he expected international regulators to be able to do, that he was seemingly unable to do inside his own lab?

I didn't get a straight answer, but my interpretation is nobody wants to apply the brakes only to see their rivals race ahead, and they don't trust each other enough to go first.

Global regulation would force them all to tow the line - and also remove some of the weight of responsibility from the industry itself.

AI is increasingly becoming a toxic brand, but in order to remind people of the benefits of the technology - and why it isn't facing an outright ban - the industry urgently needs some quick wins.

The problem is the tech sector has always been very good at promising the future, without delivering so much in the present.

And that also applies to future problems. Alarm bells rang loudly when former Anthropic safety researcher Joseph Coxon said he believed the tech had a 10% chance of destroying humanity within the next 10 years.

"There are known risks which are serious enough to be getting on with," Sir Nick Clegg, former head of global affairs at Meta, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"Whether it's bioweapons, whether it's cyber-security hacks, whether it is the implications of how people are going to be affected by an increasingly intimate and perhaps in many cases emotionally dependent relationship with AI entities going forward.

"There's enough to be really, really worried about already, without thinking that homosapiens [are] going to be eliminated by next Tuesday."

AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC

articles.title: Three leading Prem clubs in talks with overseas investors on eve of rugby union season
articles.summary: Harlequins, Saints and Gloucester attracting interest Prem using Hundred sales as template for growth Harlequins, Northampton and Gloucester are attracting serious interest from overseas investors with Prem Rugby entering an expansionist phase before its first season as a closed league begins on Friday. A source with knowledge of the discussions disclosed that there have been approaches from several high net worth individuals from the United States and the Middle East, as well as consumer brands whose interest has been piqued by Red Bull’s takeover at Newcastle last year. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Harlequins, Northampton and Gloucester are attracting serious interest from overseas investors with Prem Rugby entering an expansionist phase before its first season as a closed league begins on Friday.

A source with knowledge of the discussions disclosed that there have been approaches from several high net worth individuals from the United States and the Middle East, as well as consumer brands whose interest has been piqued by Red Bull’s takeover at Newcastle last year.

Prem Rugby’s chief executive, Simon Massie-Taylor, told the Guardian earlier this week that he expects “two or three more” deals at clubs to be completed in the next two years following the investment by Bill Foley’s Black Knight Group and James Dyson at Exeter and Bath respectively earlier this year, while US private equity company RedBird Capital Partners have had initial talks about buying a stake in the league itself.

The approach from RedBird, whose sporting portfolio includes a controlling interest in Serie A’s Milan and a minority stake in Fenway Sports Group who own Liverpool and the Boston Red Sox, has not advanced since initial informal discussions first took place in July with Prem Rugby focused on deepening their collaboration with existing private equity partners CVC Capital, but investment talks with several clubs are understood to be continuing apace.

As the closest Prem club to central London with The Stoop within 15 minutes of Heathrow, Harlequins’ attraction to overseas investors is obvious, although they have struggled on the field in recent years, finishing second-bottom last season and not reaching the playoffs since 2022.

Quins’ turnover is the highest in the Prem at almost £30m, but in their most recently published accounts covering the 2024-25 season they posted pre-tax losses of £3.5m.

Long-term owner Duncan Saville appointed himself to the board after almost 30 years at Quins earlier this year, and may be open to fresh investment.

Champions Northampton are also believed to be attracting plenty of interest after winning two titles in the last three years and they have England’s most marketable player in Henry Pollock, who this week signed a new long-term contract at the club.

Northampton’s success has come despite the club’s spending coming in at significantly below the Prem’s £6.4m salary cap, which enabled them to cut their annual losses from £1m to £700,000 in 2024-25 in another sign of a well-run operation.

Gloucester would represent more of a rescue mission as their losses increased significantly from £516,000 to £2.91m in their accounts to June 2025, leading chief executive Alex Brown to take the unusual step of publicly confirming they are looking for investment. “There is interest in Gloucester Rugby, but our shareholders and board are very sensitive to who that investment might be,” he said. “It has to be right for the club. Talks are ongoing about further investment.”

None of the 10 Prem clubs are understood to be profitable. A report from accountancy company Leonard Curtis published last year put their combined losses at £34m for the 2023-24 season, a 40% increase on the previous 12 months, with six of the clubs losing at least £3m.

The Prem’s decision to scrap promotion and relegation until at least the 2029-30 season however, has given wealthy individuals and funds confidence that the sport is worth investing in, particularly in the US given the country’s culture of closed franchise leagues.

With AFC Bournemouth’s owners, Black Knight, having paid around £25m for Exeter during the summer, the valuations are also attractive to American buyers given US franchises in all sports – both men’s and women’s – routinely have asking prices running into hundred of millions of dollars.

Prem Rugby’s plans to expand to 12 teams in 2029 has also created investment opportunities elsewhere, with an expansion to the midlands via the reborn Worcester Warriors, who have joined the second-tier Champ for first time since entering administration four years ago, and a potential new team in Birmingham the main focus.

As revealed by the Guardian in February, Birmingham City’s owners, Knighthead Capital, have expressed interest in acquiring a rugby team as the next stage of its multisport strategy that has seen it buy a 49% share in the Birmingham Phoenix Hundred franchise and a majority share in Netball Super League club Birmingham Panthers.

The Raine Group, the US bank that ran the Hundred sales process, is providing strategic advice to Prem Rugby. The England and Wales Cricket Board’s success in raising £520m for English cricket is acting as the template according to several sources charged with targeting investors.

articles.title: Pumpkin, pecan, quince, apple or plum: Adriann Ramirez’s autumn pie recipes
articles.summary: The pastry chef gives autumn’s best ingredients a golden glow-up I have come to adore what the British autumn brings: beautiful apples, pumpkins, plums and quince galore. These pies not only sing the praises of this bounty, but put them front and centre. I also use ingredients such as piloncillo (a Mexican raw cane sugar), tonka bean (which adds a beautiful fig-leaf flavour) and buckwheat flour (for a wonderfully nutty taste). These aren’t always easy to find, but they are worth the extra effort, taking these bakes to the next level. Continue reading...
articles.content:
I have come to adore what the British autumn brings: beautiful apples, pumpkins, plums and quince galore. These pies not only sing the praises of this bounty, but put them front and centre. I also use ingredients such as piloncillo (a Mexican raw cane sugar), tonka bean (which adds a beautiful fig-leaf flavour) and buckwheat flour (for a wonderfully nutty taste). These aren’t always easy to find, but they are worth the extra effort, taking these bakes to the next level.

For the pie dough 90g cold water 30g apple cider vinegar 375g plain flour , plus extra for dusting 50g caster sugar 5g tab le salt 250g cold butter, cut into 6 chunks 1 egg, beaten, for brushing Double cream, lightly whipped, to serve

For the filling 200g double cream 115g whole milk 3 medium-sized eggs (170g) 300g grated pi lconcillo (panela), or brown sugar 50g maple syrup 425g tinned pumpkin 1 tbsp vanilla extract 1 tbsp rum 2 tsp ground cinnamon 2 tsp mixed spice A few gratings fresh nutmeg A few gratings tonka bean

Combine the water and vinegar in a container and put in the freezer for about 10 minutes, until cold.

Meanwhile, put the dry ingredients for the dough in the bowl of a stand mixer and whisk to combine. Add the butter and, using the paddle attachment, mix on slow until it has broken down but some medium-large (flattened) pieces remain. (To do this by hand, use your fingertips to rub the butter into the flour.)

Add the water/vinegar and mix again until it just comes together into a shaggy dough. Turn out on to a floured surface and bring the last bits together with your hands.

Using a rolling pin, flatten into a rough rectangle, cut into four equal pieces and stack the pieces on top of each other. Flatten into a rectangle again and repeat this process once more. Chill for one hour.

Once chilled, flour the work surface and dough, and roll it into a 25cm circle, roughly 3mm thick . Gently press the dough into a 23cm loose-bottomed pie tin, folding the overhang under itself to create a small edge. Using two fingers, push the edge in the opposite direction to crimp. Freeze for 15 minutes.

Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5. Line the pastry with scrunched up baking paper, fill with rice or baking beans, then bake for 15 minutes. Remove the rice/baking beans and parchment paper, and return to the oven for a further 10 minutes. Brush with the beaten egg and bake for a further five minutes to seal.

Turn the oven down to 150C (130C fan)/300F/gas 2. To make the filling, mix all the ingredients in a bowl with a whisk, until combined. Pour into the pie crust and bake for 45-50 minutes, until there is only a slight wobble to the filling.

Let the pie cool completely in the tin, then transfer to the fridge to chill. Serve cold with lightly whipped double cream.

For the dough 140g unsalted butter, softened 85g icing sugar 1 medium-sized egg 45g buckwheat flour 175g plain flour, sieved (plus extra for dusting) 30g ground almond 15g cocoa powder

For the filling 150g granulated sugar 155g maple syrup 165g golden syrup 2 tbsp rum 1 tbsp sea salt 1 tsp vanilla extract 1 tsp ground cinnamon Zest of ½ orange 55g cold unsalted butter 3 medium eggs (170g), lightly beaten 300g pecan halves In a stand mixer with the paddle attachment, beat the butter and icing sugar for three minutes, or until light in colour. Add the egg and beat until combined.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the buckwheat and plain flour, ground almond and cocoa powder, then combine with the egg mixture.

Pat the dough into a round disc, wrap in clingfilm and refrigerate for at least an hour.

Lightly flour the work surface and dough, then roll out the dough to about 2.5cm larger than a 20cm loose-bottomed tart tin. Gently fold the dough in half, then fold in half again and place it in your tin. Gently unfold it and begin to press the dough into your tin – if it tears, just gently push it back together. Freeze for 15 minutes.

Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 . Fill the tart shell with crumpled baking paper and baking beans, and bake for 15 minutes. Remove the paper and beans, and bake for another five minutes. Leave to cool.

Meanwhile, make the filling: combine the sugar, syrups, rum and salt in a saucepan, and cook over a medium heat until it begins to boil. Continue cooking for another minute.

Take off the heat and add the vanilla, cinnamon, orange zest and butter, stirring until just combined. Let it come to room temperature, then whisk in the eggs.

Spread the pecans in an even layer in the pie shell, then pour over the filling. (If you like things on the salty side, sprinkle a bit more sea salt over the top.) Bake the pie for 40-45 minutes, until the filling is just set. If the pecans are beginning to brown too quickly, gently put some foil on top and continue cooking. Serve cooled with some creme fraiche.

For the pie dough 90g cold water 30g apple cider vinegar 375g plain flour , plus extra for dusting 50g caster sugar 5g tab le salt 250g cold butter, cut into 6 chunks 1 egg, beaten, for brushing

For the filling 500g crisp apples, like Rosette , Discovery or Jazz 200g quince 50g caster sugar 1 tbsp vanilla extract 2 tsp ground cinnamon 2 tbsp plain flour A sprinkle of sea salt Juice of 1 lemon A few gratings of nutmeg

For the crumble 200g plain flour 175g dark brown sugar 25g demerara sugar 1 tbsp ground cinnamon 1 tsp table salt 150g unsalted butter, cold and cubed 100g pecans, roughly chopped

Combine the water and vinegar for the dough in a container and put in the freezer for about 10 minutes, until cold.

Put the dry ingredients in the bowl of a stand mixer and whisk to combine. Add the butter and, using the paddle attachment, mix on slow until it has broken down but some medium-large (flattened) pieces remain. (To do this by hand, use your fingertips to rub the butter into the flour.)

Using a rolling pin, flatten the dough into a rough rectangle, cut into four equal pieces and stack the pieces on top of each other. Flatten into a rectangle again and repeat this once more. Chill for one hour.

Flour the work surface and dough, and roll it out into a 25cm circle, roughly 3mm thick. Press the dough gently into a 23cm loose-bottomed pie tin, and with the overhang, fold it under itself to create an edge. Using two fingers, push it in the opposite direction to create a crimped edge, then freeze for 15 minutes.

Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5. Line the pastry with scrunched up baking paper, fill with baking beans and blind bake for 15 minutes . Remove the parchment and beans, and bake for a further 10 minutes; leave to cool.

Meanwhile, peel and core the apples and quince. Cut the apples in quarters then thinly slice them; grate the quince. Toss the fruits in a bowl with the remaining filling ingredients, and leave to macerate while you make the crumble topping.

Using a stand mixer with the paddle attachment, mix all the dry crumble ingredients. Add the cubed butter and mix until it just begins to clump – do not overmix or it will become a solid dough. Toss in the pecans and mix by hand.

Spread the fruit mix evenly on the baked dough, then top with the crumble mix. Bake at 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 for 40-45 minutes, until the crumble is firm and the fruit slowly bubbles underneath. Serve hot with freshly whipped cream or ice-cream, and custard, too, if you’re nasty like me.

For the pie dough 180g cold water 60g apple cider vinegar 750g plain flour 100g caster sugar 10g tab le salt 500g cold butter, cut into 12 chunks

For the filling 1kg plums, your favourite variety (I love pluots ). 100g caster sugar ¼ tsp ground cinnamon ¼ tsp ground ginger A pinch of ground cloves A pinch of ground nutmeg 1 vanilla pod, split in half and the seeds scraped out Juice of 1 lemon A pinch of salt 3 tbsp cornflour Double cream, for glazing and serving Demerara sugar, for sprinkling

Put the dry ingredients for the dough in the bowl of a stand mixer and whisk to combine. Add the butter and, using the paddle attachment, mix on slow until it has broken down but some medium-large (flattened) pieces remain. (To do this by hand, use your fingertips to rub the butter into the flour.)

Macerate the plums by cutting them into quarters (if they’re large plums, cut into eighths) and putting in a bowl with the sugar, spices, vanilla, lemon juice, salt and cornflour. Combine and leave for 30 minutes.

Drain the plums, putting the liquid in a saucepan over a medium heat. Whisk until it begins to boil, then continue cooking, stirring, for a further minute. The liquid will be very thick and glossy.

Add the now-thickened liquid back to the plums and mix gently. Taste and add more sugar, lemon or spice, if needed; set aside to cool completely.

Roll out the two separate pieces of dough to the shape of your baking tray (I use a 25cm x 20cm one, with at least 3cm height) with at least 2.5cm excess on the sides. Chill in the fridge for 30 minutes.

Take one piece of dough and line the tray with it, pressing the dough firmly into the sides of the tray, then lightly prick the base with a fork. Crumple up a piece of baking paper to make it more pliable, flatten it, then use this to line the dough, and use this to line the dough, adding baking beans on top. Blind bake at 190C (170C fan)/gas 5 for 15 minutes, then remove the beans and parchment, and continue baking for another eight minutes. Set aside to cool.

Tip in the filling and spread evenly. Using a pastry brush, brush the edges of the cooked pastry with cream, then top with the second piece of dough, gently crimping your edges. Brush the lid with more double cream and sprinkle with demerara sugar. Make two slits in the lid and bake for 40-45 minutes, until the top is golden brown and the filling slow bubbling. Serve hot with creme fraiche, ice-cream or whipped cream.

Turn the oven down to 150C (130C fan)/300F/gas 2. To make the filling, mix all the ingredients in a bowl with a whisk, until combined. Pour into the pie crust and bake for 45-50 minutes, until there is only a slight wobble to the filling.

Add the egg and beat until combined.
In a separate bowl, whisk together the buckwheat and plain flour, ground almond and cocoa powder, then combine with the egg mixture.
Pat the dough into a round disc, wrap in clingfilm and refrigerate for at least an hour.

articles.title: When and how to see the Harvest Moon in 2026
articles.summary: September's full Moon will rise across on Saturday 26 September. The best viewing conditions currently look to be across southern and eastern parts of the UK.
articles.content:
September's full Moon will be visible in UK skies this weekend, just days after the autumn equinox.

Known as the Harvest Moon, it will reach its fullest point at 17:49 BST on Saturday 26 September.

At that time it will still be below the horizon for much of the UK, but it will rise shortly afterwards and appear almost completely full throughout Saturday evening.

It gets its name from being the full Moon closest to the autumn equinox, which this year took place on Wednesday.

September's full Moon is traditionally associated with the harvest, because historically, the additional moonlight after sunset was useful to farmers gathering crops.

The Royal Observatory Greenwich also lists the Corn Moon as another common name, reflecting the crops traditionally harvested around this time of year.

However, it does not always fall in September and if October's full Moon is closer to the autumn equinox, it takes the title instead.

The 2025 Harvest Moon, seen here rising over the City of London, was on 7 October

If you catch the Moon as it rises it may appear yellow, orange or even reddish.

This is not a special feature of the Harvest Moon, but simply that when it lies low in the sky and is close to the horizon, its light has to travel through more of the Earth's atmosphere before reaching our eyes.

More of the shorter blue wavelengths of light are scattered, allowing the yellows, oranges and reds to become more prominent.

A pilot boat passes the rising Harvest Moon in 2021 off Swanpool Beach, Falmouth

Many parts of the UK will have favourable conditions for viewing the Harvest Moon, with the longest clear spells expected in the south and east

The current forecast suggests Saturday could bring some drier and brighter weather, particularly across parts of England. However, there is some cloud further west and rain for parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland by the evening.

The best chance of clearer skies currently looks to be across some southern and eastern parts of the UK, while conditions are expected to be more changeable elsewhere.

The exact times of the moonrise will vary across the UK but will be shortly after it reaches its fullest point.

Keep up to date with the weather where you are online or on the BBC Weather app.

At least seven months of relentless rain needed to end drought, research shows

articles.title: Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes
articles.summary: The proposals would also see benefits cut for people who are able to work but have failed to hold down a job.
articles.content:
The Conservatives have promised to prevent long-term jobless benefit claimants from spending their welfare payments on alcohol, cigarettes and gambling.

Under the party's proposals, claimants who have been unemployed for more than six months would see their Universal Credit cut by 30% if they have not previously paid enough into the system, despite being able to work.

This reduced rate would be paid onto a "Back to Work" card, which would not allow cash withdrawals or spending on these items.

The Tories said the proposals were designed to encourage people back into work and cut the soaring welfare bill but Labour branded the scheme "unworkable".

A Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives had 14 years to fix our welfare system but they completely failed to make meaningful reforms.

"Now they are proposing an unworkable new card scheme, which does nothing to tackle the numbers of people their system left signed off and written off."

Reform proposes £50bn welfare bill cut with changes to disability payments for millions

The Tories estimate the proposed changes would move about 350,000 claimants onto the lower rate of Universal Credit, saving around £538m a year.

Under the proposals, anyone fit to work would get six months on full benefits to find a job.

Every two years a claimant has previously worked would buy an extra year on the full rate of Universal Credit - but those who have not contributed enough would drop to a new "subsistence allowance", worth 70% of the full rate.

The party said this would protect "those with a strong employment record".

For example, a 58-year-old who has worked since leaving school but has been made redundant would keep the full allowance up to state pension age.

Claimants who are sick, disabled or already in work would also be exempt, with only those judged capable of work affected.

The Tories said the reduced subsistence allowance would be loaded onto pre-paid card that would not allow cash withdrawals, and would "prevent spending" on alcohol, cigarettes, or gambling.

The party is yet to detail how its proposal would work, but shadow welfare secretary Helen Whately said it would be "a version" of the pre-paid Aspen card issued to asylum seekers living in government-funded accommodation.

These cards cannot be used to make contactless, telephone or internet payments, whilst asylum seekers whose applications have failed cannot withdraw cash.

The Home Office confirmed last year it had tightened the list of permitted retailers where the cards can be used, after reports that some asylum seekers had used the cards to gamble in sites such as slot machine arcades.

Whately said the party would also look to learn from Australia, where certain claimants are issued with debit cards that restrict purchases , external at shops selling alcohol, tobacco products or pornography.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the current system "where someone who can work chooses not to, and earns more benefits than someone in a job" was "unfair".

"The best welfare is a well-paid job. So, we will be tough on those who exploit the system because the current system is unfair to workers, taxpayers and those who truly need support," she said.

"Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can't be bothered."

However, Helen Barnard, director of policy and research at the anti-poverty charity Trussell, said the proposals were "deeply misguided".

"Universal Credit already falls well short of what people need to afford the essentials like food and heating, forcing people across the UK to the doors of food banks," she said.

"We see people's health being damaged and their ability to find and maintain work undermined by the severe hardship so many are facing."

Reform UK's economy spokesman, Robert Jenrick, said the Tories had left record numbers on long-term benefits and the proposals "won't even put a dent" in the welfare bill.

The Conservatives have already pledged to scrap Personal Independence Payment, the main disability benefit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, for "low-level" mental health conditions to help cut the welfare bill.

The party also wants to make it harder to claim sickness benefits, which it said would mean more people are required to look for work.

Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to £408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has insisted he will get the welfare bill down, for example by tackling the number of young people not in education, employment or training, but not through "crude cuts".

articles.title: Have Arsenal been figured out? Three big questions after Brighton’s upset
articles.summary: This week, we dive into the big questions surrounding the most surprising result of the Premier League weekend Before this past weekend, Arsenal had not lost in the Premier League since April. Nine straight league wins had been enough to crown the Gunners as champions at the end of last season and firmly establish them as the team to beat early this season. Against Brighton on Saturday, though, the team to beat were beaten. Thoroughly. Continue reading...
articles.content:
This week, we dive into the big questions surrounding the most surprising result of the Premier League weekend

B efore this past weekend, Arsenal had not lost in the Premier League since April. Nine straight league wins had been enough to crown the Gunners as champions at the end of last season and firmly establish them as the team to beat early this season.

Against Brighton on Saturday, though, the team to beat were beaten. Thoroughly.

Arsenal weren’t just pecked by the Seagulls . They were pressed to death by them. Usually so resilient, even in the face of such opposition exuberance, the Premier League champions fell apart on the south coast, losing a match by three goals for the first time in over three years. It was jarring to see Arsenal so out of sorts.

Was this simply a Control-Alt-Delete game for Arsenal , or has the manner of the Seagulls’ performance provided a template for others to use? Was Saturday merely a blip that the Gunners will quickly recover from or the first crack in their previously impenetrable armour? Let’s tackle those and some other questions from the Premier League’s big upset before the international break.

The most effective element of Brighton’s performance was their relentless pressing of Arsenal in periods of settled possession. While the Seagulls still had pressing triggers which prompted them to push high up the pitch at certain moments, Fabian Hürzeler also recognised the need to prevent the champions from getting to the edge of the box. They were in Arsenal’s faces for most of the match.

Brighton defensive midfielder Chema Andrés pushed up on to Martin Ødegaard whenever he could, moving Brighton into a man-to-man shape against the ball and limiting the Norwegian whenever he dropped deep. Faced with a four-on-four situation in build-out, Arsenal simply weren’t sharp enough on the ball to get around the press, forcing David Raya to go long more times than he would have liked. From there, Brighton could turn the ball over and attack at speed in the other direction.

This made the match a transition-heavy affair which suited Brighton’s attacking players. Focal point Charalampos Kostoulas was an all-round threat while Pascal Gross, Maxim De Cuyper and Diego Gómez were impactful in open space. Hürzeler’s approach never allowed the game state to shift in Arsenal’s favour. He covered all bases.

Maybe, but it will be tough. Hürzeler’s team are a physical force of nature. Of the four players that covered the most distance on Saturday, three were Brighton players and it’s these legs and lungs that allows them to press so hard for so long. No Premier League team is averaging more high turnovers per 90 minutes this season. Not every team can do what Brighton do.

For all that Brighton’s approach as a team, and a club, epitomises the modern game, there was an old school quality to the way they disrupted Arsenal. “We wanted to win the small battles first,” explained Hürzeler on talkSport, revealing the instructions he gave his players. “Win the first header, win the first tackle, win the first throw-in, win the first corner.”

Probably not, since there were some mitigating factors that explain Arsenal’s underperformance. The trip to Brighton was their fourth away game in just 10 days, and their general lethargy reflected this. Furthermore, many of Arsenal’s best players, including Martin Ødegaard, Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka, were denied a pre-season due to their extended involvement at the World Cup.

Two of Brighton’s three goals came from low-xG shots from outside the box. Arsenal were guilty of not closing the space for the shooter quickly enough, but on another day Gross and Kostoulas would have shot over the bar rather than into the top corner. Indeed, Brighton’s three goals came from a total xG of just 1.31, less than Arsenal’s xG of 1.63.

Arsenal are also still without the injured William Saliba whose presence next to Gabriel Magalhaes surely would have steadied their defensive line. Without Ben White in the lineup, the Gunners additionally lacked the chemistry down the right wing that has been such a feature of their early-season success. Saka was a non-factor in the game.

Many predicted Arsenal would stroll this season’s title race. They still might. While Manchester City are now top of the table, Arsenal are two points better off now than they were at the same stage of last season when they went on to win the title for the first time since the Arsène Wenger era. Until Saturday, they had won seven out of seven in all competitions this season. Mikel Arteta need not panic.

You can bet, however, that the tactical analysts and data crunchers employed by Arsenal’s rivals will have closely watched Brighton’s 3-0 win more than a few times by the time club soccer resumes next month.

articles.title: Infantino under pressure to include abandoned World Cup sell-off plan in external Fifa review
articles.summary: Council members also want Balogun affair included Fifa president says review letter been well received Fifa council members will demand that Gianni Infantino include the abandoned World Cup sell-off plan and the Folarin Balogun affair in his proposed external review of Fifa’s governance. In a letter sent to all 211 of Fifa’s member associations on Monday, Infantino said he would ask the council to commission a review of “Fifa’s current governance framework for major strategic initiatives” at its next meeting, in Zurich on 15 October, but he faces an internal battle over its terms of reference. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Fifa council members will demand that Gianni Infantino include the abandoned World Cup sell-off plan and the Folarin Balogun affair in his proposed external review of Fifa’s governance.

In a letter sent to all 211 of Fifa’s member associations on Monday, Infantino said he would ask the council to commission a review of “Fifa’s current governance framework for major strategic initiatives” at its next meeting, in Zurich on 15 October, but he faces an internal battle over its terms of reference.

The Football Association’s chair, Debbie Hewitt, wrote to Infantino last week demanding the release of all documents relating to the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme that was abandoned last month, as well as the background to the global governing body’s decision to lift Balogun’s suspension during the World Cup, a request that has the support of many fellow council members.

One told the Guardian that without a retrospective analysis of FFE and Balogun, any governance review would lack credibility. Another suggested Infantino was seeking to avoid personal scrutiny by offering to look at Fifa’s governance structures moving forward rather than past controversies.

The council is made up of 28 representatives of the six confederations, eight vice-presidents, Infantino and Fifa’s secretary general, Mattias Grafström.

In the immediate aftermath of the Balogun affair, when the US striker’s suspension from the World Cup last-32 tie against Belgium was lifted after a phone call to Infantino from Donald Trump , a group of council members attempted to call an extraordinary general meeting but were unable to get the 19 votes required.

The European, Asian and North and Central American and Caribbean confederations campaigning against Infantino have 21 of the 38 council seats between them, but that includes delegates from Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Malaysia, who have issued public statements of support for the president.

The German football federation president, Bernd Neuendorf, expressed the European view clearly this week by describing Infantino’s offer of a governance review as cynical electioneering, but any vote on the matter at the council is likely to be tight.

“I regard Gianni Infantino’s letter as a transparent ploy to secure ⁠his re-election next year,” Neuendorf said. “Fundamentally, Fifa now seems to have recognised that changes are essential. However, Gianni Infantino ⁠is definitely not the right person to lead a reform ⁠process.”

Infantino said on Wednesday his letter had been well received. He was speaking while attending the opening night of the Arabian Gulf Cup in Jeddah, from where he will fly to New York for meetings at the United Nations general assembly.

“I am looking forward to receiving feedback from everyone, following my letter,” he said. “I have received positive messages about it from different parts of the world, and it is important that we keep listening to each other, here in Saudi Arabia, in any one of Fifa’s 211 member associations.

“We have a council meeting next month, so we will continue to have dialogue on these important matters. There must be a culture of dialogue, of listening to each other and respecting each other.

“This is not about generating positive headlines, it is about doing what is right for the game. And I have never been more determined and committed in doing that. Fifa is always engaged. I am always engaged and want to hear how we can continue to grow football for the benefit of everybody, everywhere.”
