articles.content:
Shortcuts work against the rewards of friendship: authentic relationships can surely only be forged when you’re not expecting a return on your money

W hat price would you put on friendship? In these hyper-capitalistic times, where nothing is beyond being given a monetary value, perhaps even Mastercard wouldn’t dare to claim that it’s priceless. A YouGov survey found that 15% of Britons say they have no close friends, while nearly one in 10 (8%) have no friends at all. The numbers are similarly dismal in the US. As we face this contemporary crisis of connection, it is little wonder that friendship, or at least the possibility of it, is increasingly being marketed for sale.

There has been a striking increase in online platforms and apps that promise to introduce you – algorithmically, through social mixers or a combination – to your next BFF. There’s Cliq , PLY , standing for “People Like You”, and RealRoots which promises user satisfaction with the tagline: “Make new friends. Guaranteed”. Meanwhile, 222 boldly declares it is “not a friend-making service”, but a means to “explore serendipity” through social experiences with compatible people.

And this new sweep of pay-to-play friendships doesn’t stop at apps and algorithmic matchmaking. It is accompanied by supper clubs, book clubs, running clubs and other opportunities for you to mingle with people in your area – for a fee, of course. CircleUp , for example, holds regular social mixers across the UK for paying members, so that you can “keep seeing the same faces”. Others cultivate a more exclusive crowd. Gathering Tables hosts dinners for a “curated mix of guests”, united by their willingness to pay £145 a head.

These initiatives dangle community, but whether this trumps their commercial reason for being is debatable. The price of these apps and events is sometimes framed as a means of securing commitment, not just covering costs. “When you do things for free, people often don’t turn up,” PLY’s founder told the Guardian . But the effort becomes less civic-minded when you consider the desire for friendship is what makes these services valuable in the first place. These friend-making apps and paid-for gatherings may well offer opportunities for social connection – they are at least a date in the diary. But make no mistake, they exist primarily to encourage investment in a brand and even create opportunities to spend. Of course it is possible to make genuine connections in commercial spaces – many of us have made close bonds at work – but paying for introductions feels antithetical to the spirit of true friendship.

This new commercial interest in facilitating “gathering” speaks to the sense of collective untethering from community. Many of us understand we are lacking community, perhaps even more than friendship. It is unsettlingly common to hear people complaining of their current social network, as though a more suitable or nourishing one already exists, just waiting for you to slot into it. No wonder brands are attempting to package them up.

Cliq claims the first step to “start your community” is to download its app. But real community is built, not bought (and certainly not downloaded). It takes time, shared investment and often some weathering on both sides . It is certainly possible that meaningful, enduring ties can begin at a paid-for meet-up. But while the payment can create the conditions for friendship, it can’t manufacture the friendship itself.

Tellingly, ease is often central to the offering: Cliq claims “finding your people shouldn’t be difficult”. Shouldn’t it? No matter how you meet, it takes time and effort to turn an acquaintance into a friend; that same process, multiplied and sustained, is what creates a community. Seeking shortcuts or higher-quality connections is not only beside the point, it works against the rewards: authentic relationships can only be forged without expectation of a return on investment.

That’s not to say we don’t need more places and opportunities to meet new people; the very existence of these services at least demonstrates that we do. But before entrusting our need for greater intimacy and affection to a third party, we might ask ourselves if we could be doing more to put ourselves out there socially. Could we extend an invitation to friendly strangers, or introduce our mutuals and turn acquaintances into friends?

The best community-building exercise I’ve heard of lately was before a performance of Austentatious – the Jane Austen comedy play – where all solo ticket-holders were invited to come early and mingle before the show. The event was free, organised around a preexisting commitment and people could opt in. There was the opportunity to meet people; the work, and potential reward, of making a new friend was left to you.

articles.title: Kim Kardashian’s Team Moms highlights the ridiculous excess of the US youth-sports industry
articles.summary: A new Paramount+ series premiering Thursday turns pushy sports parents into glossy entertainment – with the children largely ushered off stage Remember when pushy sports parents were deserving objects of our collective scorn? When Marv Marinovich and Jim Pierce were bywords for abusive fatherhood, Sarah Palin made the overbearing hockey mom a global punchline, and grim stories of pushy parents assaulting officials , kids and one another grabbed headlines and trained a harsh spotlight on youth sports ? Well, the rebrand is in full swing. Team Moms: Baseball is a glossy new reality series premiering Thursday that aims to recast the pushy sports parent as something well worth coveting, a sexy black hat with a designer label. From the makers of Love Island (ITV America), for Hollywood’s most rapacious studio (Paramount Skydance), with none other than basketball mom Kim Kardashian attached as executive producer, the Paramount+ series follows a cluster of parents whose sons attend Legendary Prep Academy – a Scottsdale, Arizona baseball hothouse with an intense focus on cultivating diamond gems. Anyone coming to this expecting genuine insights on a $40bn industry that’s now under siege from private equity , swallowing ever larger chunks of hard-earned family budgets along the way, should know up front: this is a closer cousin to Bravo’s Real Housewives franchise than ESPN’s 30 for 30. Continue reading...

The title alone – a deliberate play on Teen Mom, MTV’s train-wreck young-mothers series – gives the game away. It makes abundantly clear that the focus of Team Moms’ eight hour-ish episodes isn’t the 13- and 14-year-olds chasing their field of dreams. It’s the middle-aged parents chasing vicarious glory, proximal clout and social validation. The tone is reinforced at the start of the show, in an around-the-horn-style opening title sequence that punctuates family portraits with the kids’ heroic glove work before landing on baseball cards of the individual moms fanned out over home plate. Never mind that the moms are set up to be the fall guys for the real drama queens: the dads.

The Kardashian-meets-Love Island alchemy is undeniable in the way Team Moms presents staggering opulence as wholly incidental: the luxury car fleets, the giga-mansions, the immaculate show kitchens that provide the backdrop for daily routines and gossip. The kids move through this world as you’d expect of kids who essentially have baseball for a job, zombieing themselves from bed to a hot cup of coffee before shuffling off into the predawn for another shift at the ballpark salt mines. For inspiration, the kids only need look to the writing on the walls: Prefer pain. Comfort is a slow death. Die growing, pledge growth to the grave . Upton Sinclair, eat your heart out .

It’s a five-days-a-week grind before you even get to weekend games – many of which demand hours of commuting – or the additional baseball “tutoring” many of these families seek out in hopes of keeping their kids on a steady development curve or outpacing their peers. The same can hardly be said of the academic side of this equation, which doesn’t appear to take up more than a few hours of the training day if the players even have energy left to get it at all. Producers can barely be bothered to ask about the obvious toll of this grind in the gratuitous kiddie confessionals, much less get them to consider the prospect of taking up other sports – something many great athletes do, as my former Sports Illustrated colleague David Epstein explores in his 2019 book Range .

Of course none of this athletic hothousing comes cheap. Legendary Prep doesn’t publicize its tuition costs, but I suppose you’re already in trouble if you even have to ask. Similar academies charge anywhere from $12,000 to more than $20,000 annually for the same basic bundle of high-level athletic training, sports science analytics, team travel and a hybrid or supervised online academic curriculum. There was no explicit mention of tuition costs in the three-ish episodes of Team Moms that I watched, but one mom did let slip that she bought her 16-year-old daughter a Porsche Macan to somewhat offset the money the family spends on her brother’s baseball prospects.

While this same mom – we’ll call her Pilates Mom because the names on this show aren’t as important as the archetypes – bankrolls her boy’s dream despite her keen awareness of his having “a 0.02% chance” of making it to the MLB, the other parents in the series are quite convinced they have the next Aaron Judge or Bryce Harper on their hands. (With names like Jett and Stryker, how could these kids miss?) All the families are white, and the irony of their sons of privilege chasing an MLB dream that so many less-resourced Latin American kids pursue, with relatively outsized success , is completely lost on them (even though that pipeline has its leaky bits , too).

We’re meant to view Pilates Mom as the villain because she swans around in athleisure wear that accentuates her curves and draws snide remarks. Pilates Mom sets tongues wagging after offhandedly calling one boy “a little bitch” during one of her Pilates sessions with the kids – the same boy had told her son he watches Pilates Mom on OnlyFans, prompting a schoolyard dustup.

Team Mom fault lines are drawn in hair dye. On one side, there’s the cliquey blondes: Martha Stewart Mom, the type-A who leaves her husband a “How to Be Me” memo when she steps away from the house; Party Mom, living her best life in retirement with streaks; and Trophy Mom, a Nascar wife who cites marriage and motherhood as her biggest accomplishments. On the other, the slightly more self-aware brunettes: Pilates Mom, often shot inside her empty studio; Wine Mom, the wary wife of a hobby vintner; and Friends Mom, a Courteney Cox lookalike whose coming-out story and enduring friendship with her fogey ex-husband frustrate the parent group into making crude jokes about her “returning to the other side of the pond”.

But the women and their drama just provide cover for their pushy sports spouses. A group spring break trip has Wine Dad torn over whether to let his son, a flashy teen who seems better at branding than baseball, join his friends on a kayaking excursion or drive him an hour away for some extra hitting. (So as a compromise, they do both.) Party Dad can’t stop touting Pilates Mom’s body in mixed company. Only Nascar Dad sets a halfway decent example because Casey Mears, motor racing royalty , has actually been there, done that and is moving merch .

But the worst is Egg Dad – the Humpty Dumpty who can’t let a moment pass without mentioning he played professional hockey, even though he was no better than a minor-minor leaguer in his day. Ever irascible, he’s always threatening to drop the gloves and throw down with the moms and dads at the first sign of a funny look. Egg Dad’s son, a U14 pitcher, is relegated to the fringes of the production after breaking his forearm in a fielding collision. After Egg Mom carts him home from a hospital visit to have the surgical pins removed from his arm, Egg Dad pushes him to get back on the ball.

“I don’t even know if I could put on a glove right now,” the kid says.

“The doc says it’s up to you, but I want to see you play,” Egg Dad says.

On spring break, Egg Dad organizes a game of Plant the Flag on the gravel driveway of their Italianate resort compound – Great idea , Wine Dad says, with an eye roll – and his son winds up hurting his arm again . Egg Dad puts his poor kid on the kayak without a thought and then booze-bonds with Party Dad over how soft their two kids are. “[They’ve] got to understand the difference between a real injury and [pain] and just go,” Party Dad says. It seems no amount of Hollywood high gloss can make the stigma of the pushy sports parent disappear, even if it’s buffed and contoured by Kim K.

Likely, this won’t be the last Team Mom installment if the titular colon is any indication. You can just picture spinoffs into soccer, tennis and perhaps even the southern California youth basketball scene – where Kardashian already features prominently. Really, the fact that youth sports in the US can so easily be spun into idle entertainment tells you everything that’s wrong with a homegrown approach to athletic development that favors the paying parents over the toiling kids, or even the major college and professional clubs who have a financial incentive to turn a catch-as-catch-can approach to talent scouting into a halfway dependable, European-style conveyor belt .

And the fact that Kardashian and her producing partners intuitively know that parents would rather watch richer, better-looking versions of themselves than watch kids like theirs crash and burn while pursuing their dreams is just proof that pushy sports parents haven’t softened. They’re just reaping the benefits of softer lighting now.

articles.title: You be the judge: should my partner dial down the heat when he cooks?
articles.summary: Rhonda believes Ned ruins woks. He reckons he has famous chefs on his side. You decide whose argument is in flames • Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a juror He whacks the heat right up, which stains our wok and makes it really hard to wash up The person doing the cooking is in charge of the temperature – plus a wok is supposed to blacken Continue reading...
articles.content:
Rhonda believes Ned ruins woks. He reckons he has famous chefs on his side. You decide whose argument is in flames

He whacks the heat right up, which stains our wok and makes it really hard to wash up

My partner, Ned, does most of the cooking in our house and he’s really good at it. I help prep and I usually do the washing up, which is how this issue arose. We had an old wok that became so encrusted with burnt stir-fry it was difficult to clean. Eventually, I said we needed to buy a new wok. We bought an expensive stainless steel one, but we’ve only had it three weeks and it’s stained already.

Ned cooks with the heat turned up as high as possible. I know with a wok you turn the heat up high initially before you put in the meat or vegetables, but you’re supposed to turn it down before you add the sauces. Otherwise, they burn on to the wok and make it difficult to clean. Once you get stainless steel to a certain temperature, it maintains that heat, so you don’t need to keep the flame on maximum. The point of stainless steel is that it stays stainless. If you stain it, you’re overheating it.

Once, when Ned was cooking, I turned the heat down myself. He objected and there was a bit of argy-bargy in the kitchen. I was annoyed because I knew I would be the one scrubbing the wok later, and I had a sore shoulder.

Ned can also get distracted while cooking. He might put the rice on and then walk out of the kitchen, start reading or listening to a podcast, and forget that he needs to turn something off in five minutes. He has left the gas on before. There have even been occasions when, if I hadn’t turned the knobs down, I reckon we could have had a fire.

Ned admits he has become distracted in the past, but he won’t accept my argument about the wok. He likes to have the heat up the whole time when stir-frying and says that is the proper way to cook with a wok. I love that he does the cooking, but I’d like to avoid being burned in a fire and stay alive to eat the food – and not have to scrub the pots so hard afterward. Since I’m doing the washing up, I don’t think it’s unreasonable to ask him to turn the heat down.

The person doing the cooking is in charge of the temperature – plus a wok is supposed to blacken

I do most of the cooking and occasionally we have a stir-fry. A chef once told me that the key to making one is that you’ve got to be fast and the pan has to be “scary hot”. I also learned how to make a stir-fry from my brother-in-law, who is a chef. Preparation is essential: everything should be chopped beforehand and then added to the wok in sequence. The oil goes in, then the vegetables – we don’t eat much meat these days – and the sauces go in last. It all happens quickly and on a very high heat. It’s quite a dramatic way of cooking.

Rhonda doesn’t complain about the quality of my cooking. I don’t burn the food or the sauces, although I acknowledge we get some residue left on the pan. I think that’s an acceptable part of cooking with a wok. For me, the marks left on a wok are part of its character. They’re a testament to the cooking you’ve done. I’ve also heard Australian chef Kylie Kwong say your wok is supposed to blacken.

I’m happy to wash the wok, but I don’t think it needs to remain as shiny as it was when we bought it. And I don’t want anyone touching the knobs while I’m cooking. The person cooking has to be in charge of the temperature. If someone comes in halfway through and changes the temperature, it interferes with what I’m doing.

I accept that I have occasionally left other things cooking on a low heat and become distracted. My preferred cuisines are Italian and Indian. Indian food can cook slowly for a long time, and with Italian food I might make a sauce or ragu and let it reduce. But stir-frying is different. It’s fast and intense, and you need complete focus because it happens so quickly. To say I’m nearly burning things down is a gross exaggeration. I’m fixated on the task at hand and I like to keep the heat high. Maybe I am too focused on speed and heat sometimes, but I maintain that a wok needs to remain hot. A lightly stained wok doesn’t mean I’m cooking incorrectly.

Some food staining is normal. But Ned should get his head in the game and focus on the frying pan, lest they all end up in the fire. Pablo, 35

I’m not a chef, but growing up I was told three things about cooking. First, if you aren’t the one cooking, don’t interfere unless something is on fire (but not if they are flambéeing). Second, the person not cooking does the washing up. And finally, stainless steel rarely stays stainless. Nathan, 44

While professional chefs with seasoned carbon steel woks stir fry at speed on a high heat, it doesn’t sound like that is what Ned is doing. Staining from frequent use and stains from burned-on food are different. Maybe leaving it to soak immediately after use could resolve this issue. Jess, 37

I’m not sure having a brother-in-law who is a chef qualifies Ned as a culinarian, and staining a stainless steel pan is a waste of time (scrubbing) and money (when they eventually need to replace it). Perhaps he would benefit from taking a class – cooking, fire safety or, preferably, both. Isabella, 31

If Ned is the one who does the cooking, he should decide on the heat and the how the food is made – but Rhonda shouldn’t have to clean the wok if he makes a real mess of it. As a compromise, how about letting Ned use the wok however he chooses, as long as he also cleans it and buys the replacements? Ivy, 18

We asked whether Ahmed was right to use the money he borrowed from his sister to go on holiday.

articles.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for tomatoes stuffed with breadcrumbs, chickpeas and herbs | A kitchen in Rome
articles.summary: A well-seasoned and comforting meal to ease you into the autumn months At this time of year, baked tomatoes stuffed with rice and surrounded by a packing-chip sea of potatoes are typical all over central and southern Italy, and in many other places besides. So much so that when I see a tray of those wrinkled red caps in a bakery or canteen-like tavola calda (literally, “hot table”), it doesn’t cross my mind that the hollowed-out tomatoes underneath might be filled with something other than rice. It was only when the woman behind the counter was wrapping my two portions of cannelloni and four slices of margherita pizza that another person’s order alerted me to the fact that these tomatoes were in fact filled with breadcrumbs, chickpeas, sausage, cheese and herbs. Suddenly, the tomatoes were the most appealing item behind the steamed-up glass, and the only thing I could want. We were in Tavola Calda in Latina , just south of Rome, during the lunchtime rush, which is why I didn’t feel able to add to my order, but then I was dissatisfied with my lunch. But dissatisfaction gave me a reason to pull Claudia Roden’s A Book of Middle Eastern Food from the shelf, for her chapter dedicated to stuffed vegetables, which draws inspiration from Turkish, Uzbekistani, Azerbaijani, Armenian, Greek, Egyptian, Persian, Syrian, Lebanese, Saudi Arabian and north African recipes. Having noted that almost any vegetable can be stuffed, Roden adds that the most common filling for a hollowed-out vegetable is a well-seasoned mix of chopped onion, minced meat, rice, chopped parsley, and maybe chopped tomato; and she then goes on to give seven filling variations – some with rice, some with meat (no pork), and with various herbs and spices. She also provides a not disappointing filling including chickpeas, which is what I have adapted, also with inspiration from the busy Tavola Calda, for this week’s recipe. Continue reading...
articles.content:
A well-seasoned and comforting meal to ease you into the autumn months

A t this time of year, baked tomatoes stuffed with rice and surrounded by a packing-chip sea of potatoes are typical all over central and southern Italy, and in many other places besides. So much so that when I see a tray of those wrinkled red caps in a bakery or canteen-like tavola calda (literally, “hot table”), it doesn’t cross my mind that the hollowed-out tomatoes underneath might be filled with something other than rice. It was only when the woman behind the counter was wrapping my two portions of cannelloni and four slices of margherita pizza that another person’s order alerted me to the fact that these tomatoes were in fact filled with breadcrumbs, chickpeas, sausage, cheese and herbs. Suddenly, the tomatoes were the most appealing item behind the steamed-up glass, and the only thing I could want. We were in Tavola Calda in Latina , just south of Rome, during the lunchtime rush, which is why I didn’t feel able to add to my order, but then I was dissatisfied with my lunch.

But dissatisfaction gave me a reason to pull Claudia Roden’s A Book of Middle Eastern Food from the shelf, for her chapter dedicated to stuffed vegetables, which draws inspiration from Turkish, Uzbekistani, Azerbaijani, Armenian, Greek, Egyptian, Persian, Syrian, Lebanese, Saudi Arabian and north African recipes. Having noted that almost any vegetable can be stuffed, Roden adds that the most common filling for a hollowed-out vegetable is a well-seasoned mix of chopped onion, minced meat, rice, chopped parsley, and maybe chopped tomato; and she then goes on to give seven filling variations – some with rice, some with meat (no pork), and with various herbs and spices. She also provides a not disappointing filling including chickpeas, which is what I have adapted, also with inspiration from the busy Tavola Calda, for this week’s recipe.

I haven’t included sausagemeat in my version, but if you wish to, squeeze the meat from a couple of pork sausages and crumble it in at the same time as the chickpeas. Seasoning is fundamental here – salt, obviously (a small amount at various stages is better than all at once), as well as a little minced garlic and herbs. While my instinct here is for parsley and either rosemary or sage, dried mint also works wonderfully, as does cinnamon, whose warm, woody sweetness works beautifully with tomatoes, as it does in tomato sauce, but that’s another column.

How long the tomatoes take to bake will depend very much on their ripeness; harder ones need 10-20 minutes more than those with softer shells, but keep an eye on them and leave them to rest for a while before serving. I also think tomatoes stuffed this way benefit from being baked close together in a ceramic oven dish, which is why I baked cubed potatoes separately; some salted yoghurt or mashed courgettes or aubergine are also good accompaniments. As in the best and busiest tavole calde, serve the wrinkled tomatoes just hotter than room temperature.

8 tennis ball-sized tomatoes Salt and black pepper ½ garlic clove , minced 1 red onion , peeled and diced Olive oil 1 tbsp minced flat-leaf parsley 1 tsp minced rosemary , or mint, or ground cinnamon 200g cooked chickpeas, and/or the meat squeezed from two pork sausages 100g soft white breadcrumbs (from two-day-old bread) 2-3 tbsp grated cheese (whatever you have)

Cut the caps off the tomatoes, then use a teaspoon (and knife, if necessary) to scoop the pulp and seeds into a bowl, in order to hollow out the tomatoes.

Sprinkle the insides of the tomato shells with salt, and keep the caps. Remove any hard, white bits from the pulp/seeds, then mash the rest, seasoning with a little salt and the garlic.

In a frying pan on a medium-low heat, soften the onion in four teaspoons of olive oil with a pinch of salt. Add the herbs and chickpeas (and sausages, if using), then add the breadcrumbs, grated cheese and enough of the tomato pulp to make a soft stuffing.

Arrange the empty tomato shells in an oiled ovenproof dish, then fill them with the chickpea and breadcrumb mix. Put on the lids and bake for 30-45 minutes, or until the tomatoes are baked through, a little wrinkled and the stuffing cooked.

articles.title: Tasmania Devils line up female voice to sing team song in AFL first
articles.summary: Expansion club wants official new recording to be inclusive Selection panel will deliberate before choosing song by end of year Kylie Minogue will dazzle 100,000 fans at the MCG this weekend, but the Tasmania Devils hope there will soon be another female vocal heard on grand final day. In what would be an AFL first, the club wants to have both female and male voices on the official recording of their team song, which is expected to be selected by the end of the year. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Kylie Minogue will dazzle 100,000 fans at the MCG this weekend, but the Tasmania Devils hope there will soon be another female vocal heard on grand final day.

In what would be an AFL first, the club wants to have both female and male voices on the official recording of their team song, which is expected to be selected by the end of the year.

The Devils’ song selection panel also wants the melody to sound just as good whether it is sung by an AFL player, one from the AFLW or any supporter in the stands, and that the lyrics are inclusive of all Tasmanians.

Chief executive from the Tasmanian Symphony Orchestra, Caroline Sharpen, is part of the eight-person panel which has met three times to begin developing criteria, due to be released next month.

“One of the things that struck me in one of the very early meetings was just hearing how important it is for the team song to carry a female voice as well,” she said.

“This is a football club, the Tasmania Devils, we have AFL and AFLW teams as part of the one club, so the female vocal is going to be very much a part and a reflection of who the club actually is.”

The introduction of the AFLW a decade ago highlighted how deeply the male experience pervades football. The Western Bulldogs recorded an adaption of their song “Sons of the West” replacing “sons” with daughters”. Essendon recorded a new version of theirs sung by women with adapted lyrics, and several clubs made minor adaptations to remove or tweak gendered language.

Starting with a blank slate, the Devils’ song selection panel hopes to foreground women’s experiences. The club’s VFLW captain Meghan Gaffney, who has a decade of singing training, spent four years at GWS in the AFLW. She said she loved the Giants’ Big Big Sound , but felt that it resonated with the AFLW players less than it could have.

“When the song’s played, when you run out or when you end the game, it’s males that are singing that song,” she said. “It would be a nice feeling to be represented by a female and show that football is for men and women equally and that we don’t have to run out to a song before our game, listening to males sing.”

Gaffney said the Devils’ song will need to work in acoustically-challenged stadiums, as well as be “singable” by men and women. “It’s just where the song sits in a vocal range, so it’s easy for both men and women to sing, and it sounds good when both men and women sing or chant,” she said.

“But also, at the end of the day, the main way that this song is going to be sung is by football players and a lot of footy players aren’t musically inclined or talented, so it has to be arranged in a way that singers don’t need to be professional for the song to sound good.”

Sharpen said the panel, which also includes musical theatre performer John X and former Richmond player Matthew Richardson, found Gaffney’s perspective persuasive.

“She just spoke so articulately about her great career playing football and singing team songs that were probably written by and sung by blokes traditionally – it’s not always something that sits naturally either with the female voice, and the words don’t always include a feminine perspective,” she said.

“How can we really make sure that that’s an important part of this process and really include all of us here in Tasmania?”

There have already been more than 200 unsolicited song submissions to the club, and Up there Cazaly singer Mike Brady and Tasmanian punk band Luca Brasi have expressed an interest in penning the ditty.

The panel is expected to finalise criteria and formally call for submissions next month, before making a decision before the end of the year.

articles.title: ‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI
articles.summary: A feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting Google has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar. The most-visited site on the internet still shows the same list of links to users, but they have to scroll past a summarized response from an AI chatbot, a feature Google calls AI Overviews. The change to what was once the gateway to the rest of the internet has been profound, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting. “AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” wrote Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search, last August . In May, the company said more AI is coming . Continue reading...
articles.content:
A feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting

G oogle has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar. The most-visited site on the internet still shows the same list of links to users, but they have to scroll past a summarized response from an AI chatbot, a feature Google calls AI Overviews. The change to what was once the gateway to the rest of the internet has been profound, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting.

“AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” wrote Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search, last August . In May, the company said more AI is coming .

Google said it had not seen a decline in aggregate traffic and that such accusations are based on “flawed methodologies”. Reid, the company’s vice-president of search, wrote last year: “Total organic click volume from Google Search to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year.”

The Guardian asked readers whether Google has improved or worsened in the age of AI and how their habits of searching the internet have changed.

Better, mainly because it leads you in your quest rather than you having to search on yourself. I am happy to have the AI lead me to an answer but the mega caution is that Google AI or any of them are not at all trustworthy. I have had it admit that it was lying to me and apologise! Sionn Achog, retired teacher 76, Dublin

I find that AI responses are more informative than previously, which simply referred the user to other relevant websites. Peter Warb, 75, UK

AI has made Google better. I use AI mode for all my searches. Jose Garcia Jr , 40, recovery coach, Dallas, Texas

AI has improved Google search. The analysis and chat functions are so much more useful than a ranked list of websites that still need to be explored by the user. Reviewing a list of websites is still an option but is very time consuming, and frustrating. Alan Caruana, consultant, 62, Malta

Far more better, faster and real. I search now with confidence, complete assurance and a high degree of accuracy. Eleazar Eke, electrical engineer, 67, Onitsha, Nigeria

Much better. It hasn’t changed my behavior, just getting better and more focused results. Catherine Weber, former political analyst, 57, Oregon

It’s made Google search much better, I find that I rarely actually click on the website links any more. I find information I want much faster and have a deeper understanding of any topic as I can ask questions about it and drill into the areas I’m interested in. Mark Johnson, 52, software engineer, London

Greatly improved it by getting at more arcane info regarding subject matter. Juxtaposition has improved with AI and abstruse knowledge of subjects becomes more accessible to layman. Wonderful tool with power to extend mind through sensing connections and very akin to human thinking. Samuel Lieberstein, 90, retired teacher, Cherry Hill, New Jersey

Search has become worse. Google AI obscures sources and tries to claim information it did not create while diverting traffic from the sources it steals from. Sean Peters, document processor, 41, Portland, Oregon

Every time I search I have to scroll down to find an actual real website to find a full article or discussion or to confirm that the AI summary isn’t making things up. Occasionally when I am feeling particularly bitter, I remember to add the ““-ai”” tag to my search. Ewan Herbert, English teacher, 33, Japan

Worse. I have disabled AI overviews using an extension. Chris Gibson, Dundee

Absolutely worse. I want to be able to decide for myself which results are the most useful and relevant, and we’re no longer able to turn off the AI summary results. Jon Wilkinson, personal trainer, 43, Manchester, UK

Google has been enshittified … I do miss old Google Search and I really hope something of equal capabilities eventually comes to replace it.

The search engine I currently use is good for a lot of things, but if I need to look for something in languages other than English, the quality of the results is much lower. Image search is also not as good as that of Google used to be. Sofia, postdoctoral physics researcher, 30, Lausanne, Switzerland

My first stop now is Duck Duck Go, a pale imitation of Google’s search engine at the height of its powers. Unfortunately, the top results often include Grokipedia entries and other garbage. Craig Garrett, book editor, 52, New York City

I have stopped using Google. I now use another search engine with no AI overviews. Guy Arthur Simpson, writer 66, Spain

I’ve made a conscious effort to find a browser which does not lead with the AI results. Mine is now Ecosia. Dan Jennings, IT, 54, Southampton, UK

I do a lot of research for my studies, and the AI features are a nightmare! I’m still scouring for a decent search engine without any of these ‘AI features’, the last thing i want is to accidentally utilise a water-wasting AI behemoth datacentre when I forget that crucial suffix. I’ve even resorted to using my local library’s resource of legal cases for my work, at least it is trustworthy. Catherine O’Leary, student studying law, politics and sociology, 17, Newcastle Upon Tyne

Google has become almost useless, searches I’ve made in the past which yielded specific results, (news articles, local information, historical references) no longer appear. I no longer submit to Google search first, I go directly to Wikipedia as my first source, then to DuckDuckGo, (with AI disabled) then to Reddit and only to Google as a last resort. Pedro Reyes, 61, Galicia, Spain

articles.title: Italian pop legend takes the lead in Maria Grazia Chiuri’s Fendi collection
articles.summary: Milan show full of diaphanous dresses and visible bras celebrates ‘incredible feminist’ of the 1970s, Raffaella Carrà Maria Grazia Chiuri has been having more fun with clothes since she decamped from Paris back to her native Rome to work at Fendi. “I have less of a uniform these days. I think it is because being back here makes me feel young again. I’m not sure my daughter appreciates [this attitude]! But I don’t care,” she said at a preview before her Milan fashion week show. Not that Chiuri doesn’t approach her work as a designer seriously. She described her second ready-to-wear season at Fendi not as a show, or a collection, but as “the second part of the project I am working on for them”. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Milan show full of diaphanous dresses and visible bras celebrates ‘incredible feminist’ of the 1970s, Raffaella Carrà

Maria Grazia Chiuri has been having more fun with clothes since she decamped from Paris back to her native Rome to work at Fendi. “I have less of a uniform these days. I think it is because being back here makes me feel young again. I’m not sure my daughter appreciates [this attitude]! But I don’t care,” she said at a preview before her Milan fashion week show.

Not that Chiuri doesn’t approach her work as a designer seriously. She described her second ready-to-wear season at Fendi not as a show, or a collection, but as “the second part of the project I am working on for them”.

She is continuing the protocol she developed as the designer of Dior of using each event as a platform to celebrate women’s creativity. But instead of a ceramicist or a philosopher, her muse for this season is the Italian pop legend Raffaella Carrà.

Carrà, once described as a “one-woman Abba ”, had a Lady Gaga bob and a taste for sequined catsuits. She caused a sensation with her raunchy outfits – the first bare midriff ever seen on Italian TV, in 1970 – and her sex-positive lyrics (her song A Far L’Amore Comincia Tu translates as “Take the lead when making love”).

“She was an incredible feminist, and her relationship with her clothes was so free,” said Chiuri of Carrà, who died aged 78 in 2021.

On the catwalk, Carrà’s influence became diaphanous 1970s dresses with trailing hems, visible lace bras, embroidered waistcoats and vintage fur stoles, while men’s shirts were unbuttoned to the navel.

The biggest and starriest show of this Milan fashion week belonged not to any designer, but to Vogue. Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, Milan’s glass-domed cathedral to retail, became a catwalk for a line-up that included Jennifer Lopez in Dolce & Gabbana and Cardi B in vintage Versace, with the singer Alicia Keys and the ballet dancer Roberto Bolle performing live.

Vogue is leaning into live events to amplify its brand and strengthen its coffers as print income declines. Vogue World Milano follows last year’s Vogue World: Hollywood in LA, which generated $30m (£23m) in revenue.

Billed as a celebration of Italian craftsmanship and the human touch in fashion, the event highlighted the stark reality of an increasing dependence on benefactors from Silicon Valley.

Sponsors of the event included Meta Glasses and OpenAI, and the finale included two dancing robots, who were greeted with notably less enthusiasm by the stellar line-up of Italian designers in the front row than the rest of the show.

“The landlords have entered the chat,” read one comment beneath a video of the robots circulating on social media.

It’s natural to want to soothe eye irritation, but mishandling could lead to more problems, experts warn. We asked them for advice on how to deal with it properly

It may feel like a gritty, annoying sensation, or a sharp pain. Either way, you may have the same problem: something is stuck in your eye and needs to come out.

Addressing the situation incorrectly can lead to bigger issues such as infection, scarring, an ulcer or corneal scratches, which are abrasions on the clear covering of your eye. Ignoring the dilemma can lead to similar consequences.

Experts explain how to handle this predicament, when it’s time to see a medical professional, and some of the most common mistakes.

As innocuous as they may seem, eyelashes are some of the most common foreign bodies to get stuck in eyes. If an eyelash ends up under an eyelid, it can be quite painful, explained Dr Douglas Lazzaro, an ophthalmologist and professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine.

Other common examples Lazzaro encounters include dust and other small debris kicked up on a windy day and glue from attaching false eyelashes. Those working in construction may encounter flecks of industrial materials such as fiberglass, metal and wood.

Contact lenses are another frequent culprit, he said. These can roll up and hide under the upper eyelid, break in the eye, or may be forgotten and not removed before another is put in.

The feeling of having something in your eye can depend on the object, but general symptoms include burning and irritation, blurred vision, a scratchy feeling or sensitivity to bright lights.

For some small objects, like eyelashes, sand or mascara flecks, blinking and your own tears are often all you need to get them out.

But if that doesn’t work, you may need to do more. Wash your hands first and work in a well-lit area. Lazzaro recommends carefully examining your eye to locate whatever may be stuck. This may include gently pulling down your lower eyelid with clean fingers, or using a cotton-tipped swab to slowly lift your upper lid.

If the object is small and not penetrating your eye, blinking and irrigating the eye with artificial tears may flush the object out. If irrigation doesn’t work, then it’s likely best to seek professional attention, said Lazzaro.

If a foreign liquid gets in your eye – such as detergents and disinfectants – you’ll want to act quickly, said Dr Keith Baratz, an ophthalmologist at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota. He recommends rinsing your eye with tap water as soon as possible.

A general rule of thumb is that liquids with a high pH (for example, bleach, ammonia and most drain cleaners) are more damaging than those with a low pH – but you should hasten to rinse your eyes with tap water regardless.

“Speed is the important thing,” said Baratz. “You want to do it right away, not wait a half hour while you drive to the emergency room.”

After you rinse the eye, you should then go to the emergency room, said Dr Avnish Deobhakta, an ophthalmologist at the New York Eye and Ear Infirmary of Mount Sinai.

Experts’ advice falls into two categories. On some occasions, you should go to the doctor to remove something from your eye. There are also times when you should go even if you have been able to remove the object.

A common mistake is assuming that something in the eye will come out on its own, said Lazzaro. According to the Mayo Clinic , avoid removing anything embedded in the eye or sticking out between the lids. Doctors have tools that make the process easier: numbing drops, magnifying devices (for instance, a slit lamp microscope ) and sterile tools such as forceps or needles, which are used to dislodge particles. You should not use these tools at home, said Lazzaro.

But let’s say you removed the object and your eye still hurts. For the first 24 hours, you can continue to irrigate the eye with artificial tears, Lazzaro said. Cold compresses can also make the eye feel a little better, but don’t provide any healing benefits.

If irrigating your eye doesn’t work, and you still have “something that’s bothering you, causing vision problems, or is hard to reach”, then you “really do need to seek professional care”, said Deobhakta.

Generally, the rule is that if you don’t feel better within 24 hours – there’s still inflammation, redness, tearing or vision changes – then you should seek medical attention, said Lazzaro.

It’s possible that, when removing the object, either you caused harm or injury had already been inflicted by the object, explained Deobhakta. Another likelihood is that the injury exposed the eye to infection. A doctor can examine the wound and provide the correct aftercare, he said.

Medical care can help you avoid more than just pain; even if the foreign matter is removed, there can still be downstream effects, Lazzaro said. For example, a removed piece of wood or vegetable matter could leave behind a fungal infection . Or if a piece of metal is on the eye, rust can accumulate and become stuck to the cornea. If left untreated, this can lead to infection and scarring that can affect vision. Doctors have special instruments that brush away rust, and can follow up with an antibiotic treatment, said Lazzaro.

Rubbing the eye is heavily discouraged, said Lazzaro. If the object is still in your eye, you can “actually rub it further into your cornea”, he said. Rubbing can introduce bacteria from your hands into the eye and can also increase inflammation.

People should not use metal tools at home, like tweezers, to remove something from the eye. This can cause further injury.

“One of the worst-case scenarios is that the individual goes to a mirror and tries to pick at the foreign object with a toothpick or tweezers,” said Deobhakta.

You also don’t want to try to use your fingers to pick something out of your eye, said Baratz, adding that “this is the number one mistake we see”.

Culprits often include people who wear contact lenses and, in turn, are used to touching their eyes, he explains. But using your fingers can increase the risk of infection and injury.

Patients who wear contact lenses also tend to leave their contacts in, even if something is irritating their eyes. Another tendency is to put contacts back in immediately after an eye injury, sid Deobhakta.

“Do not put a contact lens on an eye that is already sore,” he advises. “If it’s getting better and you feel OK, use lubricating drops and wear your glasses.”

Generally, people can underestimate the inherent danger some activities pose to their eyes, said Deobhakta. He has seen patients use their glasses instead of safety goggles during a debris-causing activity such as mowing the lawn. In this case, grass can still fly up under the glasses into the eye, or a rock could hit and break the glasses, causing injury.

“Be mindful of what you’re doing, react quickly, and don’t do something silly like trying to fix the problem yourself when something does go wrong,” he says.

articles.title: Unhappy couples staying put due to cost of living crisis, say divorce lawyers
articles.summary: Financial pressures suspected to be behind figures showing failed marriages are lasting longer in England and Wales Couples are putting off divorce because of the cost of living crisis, lawyers have said, after figures showed the average length of a marriage ending in divorce in England and Wales reached a record high last year. The Office of National Statistics (ONS) released figures on Wednesday showing that the average marriage ending in divorce in 2025 lasted for 13 years. This is the longest since records began in 1963 and up from a record low of 8.9 years in 1985. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Financial pressures suspected to be behind figures showing failed marriages are lasting longer in England and Wales

Couples are putting off divorce because of the cost of living crisis, lawyers have said, after figures showed the average length of a marriage ending in divorce in England and Wales reached a record high last year.

The Office of National Statistics (ONS) released figures on Wednesday showing that the average marriage ending in divorce in 2025 lasted for 13 years. This is the longest since records began in 1963 and up from a record low of 8.9 years in 1985.

Rebecca Aston‑Jones, a senior associate at Clarke Willmott, a top law firm that specialises in divorce, said the rising cost of living was keeping unhappy couples together.

“One of the main factors discouraging people from pursuing a divorce is the significant financial pressure that comes with establishing and maintaining two separate households,” she said.

Inflation, which is rising as a result of the escalation of conflict in the Middle East, has pushed up the cost of rent, mortgages and childcare. “It is unsurprising that many people find the prospect of separation financially daunting,” Aston-Jones said.

The ONS figures show there are fewer divorces now than at their peak in the 1980s-2000s, when they reached 150,000 a year.

There were 105,002 divorces in England and Wales in 2025, made up of 102,879 opposite-sex couples and 2,123 same-sex couples. The latter figure was the highest since same-sex marriage was legalised in 2014. There were also 959 civil partnership dissolutions involving 270 opposite-sex couples and 689 same-sex couples.

The head of population life events at the ONS, Greg Ceely, said: “Divorce rates have remained stable over the past few years, but are lower than the peak levels in the 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s. Our latest findings show that people who divorce or dissolve a partnership are staying in the relationship for longer before it ends.”

That marriages were lasting longer before failing was partly down to people waiting longer before they divorced, lawyers suggested.

“As a result, some couples remain in unhappy or hostile living environments, which can be detrimental to everyone involved,” Aston-Jones said. “We are increasingly seeing couples who have separated but continue to live under the same roof so they can retain the benefit of shared assets and continue to split household expenses.

“This arrangement can often exacerbate tensions and create a more volatile home environment. We are also witnessing a growing prevalence of financial abuse within relationships, which can prevent individuals from taking the step to end their marriage because they are concerned about their ability to manage financially on their own.”

Lisa Pepper, a partner and specialist divorce lawyer at Osbornes Law, said: “Divorce is now more accessible than it ever has been in the past 60 years yet these incredible figures show that couples are staying together for a record amount of time.”

She suggested that one “less romantic reason” for marriages lasting longer was likely to be that couples were unable to afford to divorce.

“Couples are more hesitant to get divorced and trying things like mediation or couples therapy before going for the nuclear option as the consequences are often perceived as worse than continuing with their marriage,” she said.

Aston-Jones said there were cheaper ways to get divorced and that seeking advice early could help.

“There are a number of effective alternatives that can help parties reach a resolution outside of court, including mediation and arbitration,” she said. “These methods often provide quicker, more cost-effective, and practical outcomes, enabling families to move forward more amicably, which is particularly beneficial where children are involved.”

articles.title: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s approval rating: ‘somewhere between Ebola and Ed Sheeran’
articles.summary: Late-night hosts discussed the decreasing popularity of the US president and how his latest attack on the press continues to backfire Late-night hosts ridiculed Donald Trump’s disastrous approval rating and his latest rambling speech at the UN. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Late-night hosts discussed the decreasing popularity of the US president and how his latest attack on the press continues to backfire

Late-night hosts ridiculed Donald Trump’s disastrous approval rating and his latest rambling speech at the UN.

On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host spoke about Trump’s new all-time low approval rating which is “somewhere between Ebola and Ed Sheeran” at just 29%.

“If that number goes any lower, he’s gonna have to leave Melania for it,” he joked.

This week has seen the president banning CNN and MS Now from press briefings leading to other stations suspending coverage in protest.

The lack of coverage has made him “even crazier than he already is” as there is “nothing he loves more” than being on TV.

His “dumb actions” have now meant that the only camera in the White House is a “ring camera that Melania has mounted on her bedroom door to keep him out of it”.

The week also saw him meet with new UK prime minister Andy Burnham who was “visibly uncomfortable” as Trump bragged about his “very petty new attack on freedom of the press”.

But Trump’s minions have been trying to defend his actions, from JD Vance to rightwing TV pundits. Kimmel said that it’s “increasingly difficult for these hand puppets of Trump to explain the unexplainable”.

In response to the show of media solidarity that has led to Trump being removed from TV screens, he has started a “state-run media network” called Trump TV on YouTube.

It started with just 8,000 viewers, which Kimmel joked that Trump will say means “bigger ratings than the final episode of Friends”.

Kimmel also called Trumps’s UN speech “a rough, threatening, ugly ramble” that saw him brag about renaming artificial intelligence “super intelligence”.

The host said that “his legacy will be renaming things that did not need to be renamed”.

On Late Night, Seth Meyers spoke about Trump’s ribbon-cutting event at the White House this week, which had no audio as there was no press pool coverage thanks to his ban.

“You really need to learn how to project,” Meyers said as advice to the president.

Meyers said that even though we couldn’t hear what was being said, he was “either bragging or lying” and that we should “use the media as a baby monitor” when trying to check his emotional state.

Meyers also spoke about Trump’s embrace of AI, showing a picture that the president posted of himself as the pope. “We shouldn’t be building datacenters, we should be building assisted living facilities,” he said.

This week also saw Trump breaking with convention by endorsing Irish unification.

“When isn’t he breaking with decades of US precedent?” the host asked.

articles.content:
Advances in digital technology mean that avatars are ever more realistic, and zombie concerts are coming our way. Exciting as it might be to witness the Fab Four, or Maria Callas on stage, I’d rather have flesh and blood live experiences any day.

I t seems that AI’s powers – terrifyingly – know no bounds. But can it raise the dead? Here’s what Avatar concert producer Unit1 Studio’s CEO Barney Wragg said in a recent interview. “ We [are] talk[ing] about using AI to simulate the way that tears evaporate in your eye between blinks, or subcutaneous blood flow, so that when one of our [digital] characters laughs or opens their mouth or smiles, areas of their flesh will change colour as it would do in a real human”. Digital avatars are already part of our entertainment landscape – from Tupac and Abba to Maria Callas – but now that an avatar’s cheeks can change colour mid-set, is it game over for humans?

Wragg last week reported a massive investment in his company to make hyper-realistic avatar-entertainment. Unit1 plans to roll out avatars of musicians living – and dead – so that the success of Abba Voyage is just the start of a slew of “hybrid” concerts. In other words, flesh-and-blood audiences paying massive amounts of human money to witness a very expensive LED screen showing phantom musicians in the 21st century’s equivalent of the magic lantern. (The tech is a 2D illusion: you think you’re seeing Abba’s Agnetha in 3D, but you’re not; it’s all just a new-fangled but fundamentally old-fashioned trick of the light.)

And the frontiers for Wragg and his team are endless: recreating Live Aid, Hendrix at Woodstock, the Beatles at the Cavern Club, and doing so in multiple locations simultaneously.

It’s the logical endpoint of a culture of nostalgia epitomised for Wragg by his teenage nephew , who, having discovered and fallen in love with Janis Joplin’s music, wanted to see her live, but the unfortunate fact of her death in 1970 meant that this was impossible. But why should that tiny hiccup be an impediment? Unit1 can bring her back, potentially resurrecting all your other favourites of yesteryear in what Wragg calls “time-travel tourism” – assuming that they receive permission from the musicians’ estates.

Wragg talks about the tech not in terms of its creative use, but its documentary capacity: “We are re-engineering a moment in time, absolutely to fidelity. It’s not a case of interpreting what somebody said, it’s just representing exactly what they said.” Unit1’s vision goes far beyond any of classical music’s attempts to recreate the musical cultures of the past with historically informed performance practice . Wragg talks in terms of absolute fidelity to what happened, a perfect simulacrum not of a song, a symphony, or an aria, but of an actual “moment in time”, rendered as precisely as possible, to be repeated indefinitely.

Wragg admits there are limits: “We have been approached where people say, ‘What about if this person met this star?’ We’ve said, ‘Look, you’re straying into a world of fiction.’” But surely, seeing Joplin’s avatar perform as if she were still alive today is the height of science fiction. Isn’t fiction the whole point of the technology? Why not imagine Freddie Mercury singing with Ella Fitzgerald, Nat King Cole with Marlene Dietrich, or how about Mozart in a keyboard battle with Beethoven?

The problem with Mozart, Beethoven or Bach, say, is that they didn’t, alas, leave much of a digital record to work with to make their avatars, unlike Abba or Joplin. As opposed to recreating, faithfully, actual moments in time, this seems to actually be about making advanced-level digital exhibits that people will pay to see every night in spaces once reserved for human musicians to perform in but that will now be consecrated to these digital homunculi: zombie concerts, opiates for an apocalyptically nostalgic age. Try throwing an apple at the stage; try interrupting the setlist; try making them perform an encore; try to get their autographs; try to find empathy and connection with this digital playback.

Or maybe I should get with the programme and embrace the theme-park immersion of this wondrous age of technology that helps keep us stuck in a permanently perfected past. But if Unit1 could find enough digital traces out there in the ether, I’d love to have been there for the premiere of Mozart’s The Marriage of Figaro in Vienna in 1786; to have witnessed Louise Bertin’s Fausto in Paris in 1831; to be overwhelmed by Mahler’s Eighth Symphony when it was first performed in Munich in 1910; or to have been in the crowd for the premiere of Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring in Paris in 1913 to find out if there really was a riot at the ballet.

But here’s the thing. Even if Unit1 could accurately represent not only the performers but every detail of these events, it would still be meaningless as a creative project. Classical music , at least, is all about interpreting what somebody wrote in the context of our times, not recreating the same thing night after night. That’s true time travel, and there’s no AI required.

This week Tom has been listening to: Keir GoGwilt and friends’ The Zarabanda Variations , which takes a simple question – what are the origins of the dance known as the sarabande in European repertoires? – and discovers and unearths a network of stories that connect Africa to the Caribbean, European salons to the realities of colonialism, and turns all of those histories into a teeming, thrumming, retuned present tense.

articles.title: John Green got an astronomical following from his books. What came next? ‘I’m still competing for clicks’

articles.content:
Returning with his first-ever adult novel, the bestselling author reflects on fame, YouTube and his brother’s AI controversy

By his mid-30s, John Green had done pretty well for himself. His debut novel, Looking for Alaska, had won a prestigious award for young adult literature. He and his brother, Hank, had launched a popular YouTube channel, where they regularly posted videos about their lives. With their combined incomes, Green and his wife were able to cobble together a living, buying a house and starting a family in Indianapolis.

“The week that book came out, it sold more copies than all of my previous books had sold in hardcover combined,” Green recalled in a recent interview with the Guardian podcast Stateside with Kai and Carter . “Up until that moment, I’d been very cavalier about sharing my life online and offline, and it was only in the wake of that that I started to realize the cost of that. People started coming to our house, sometimes quite late at night. We had young kids – babies – back then. People don’t always have the best boundaries.”

The Fault in Our Stars follows the story of Hazel, a 16-year-old living with cancer, who falls in love with a fellow cancer patient. Powered in part by Green’s online fandom, the book sold more than 20m copies – enough for every person in the state of New York to have a copy, and then some. In 2014, Hollywood adapted it into a movie starring Shailene Woodley and Ansel Elgort. After the film became a blockbuster, raking in more than $300m at the global box office, Hollywood started adapting Green’s other books, too.

But he remains decidedly ambivalent about his popularity. It doesn’t feel nourishing, he said. It feels like empty calories.

“It was uncomfortable to talk about, because how do you not be grateful for this overwhelmingly wonderful thing in your life?” Green said. “I have a friend who’s a very successful author, and I remember she said to me once: ‘Of all the good things that ever happened to me, fame was the worst.’ I think that’s a pretty good way to think about it.”

Green decided to work through his mixed feelings in his new book, Hollywood, Ending. Released this week, the book follows two young actors who make a movie about Andy Warhol, fall in love, and try to stay sane as they sell pieces of themselves to the internet and the Hollywood publicity machine. It’s Green’s first novel in nearly a decade, and his first-ever for adults. But it still feels like a classic John Green book – thanks, predominantly, to its ardent belief that art, and other people, can help us survive anything. In an era in which more and more people must market themselves on social media, courting the dizzying highs and crushing lows of fame, Green still hopes we’ll find something better.

I spoke with Green about the moral complexity of the attention economy, what he wishes he had done differently as a pioneering YouTuber and his brother Hank’s recent AI controversy.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. Watch the Stateside podcast episode in full here .

CS: This book is so much about fame and the various machines that create and perpetuate celebrity culture: journalists, social media, movie studios. Why was this something you wanted to write about?

JG: It used to be that this was a question mostly for celebrities, mostly for actors and to a lesser extent novelists. Now, it is a question for everyone because we all participate in this attention economy. We all transform our private lives into publicly consumable goods, whether that’s posting about our dog’s death on Facebook or our marriage on Reddit or whatever. These questions about how best to handle the publicization of one’s private life are no longer rarefied.

I guess the overriding question was: is it worth it to make art in an age where art will inevitably be so commodified and will cost us so much in the making?

I feel like the moment your fame really kicked into a different gear was with the publication of The Fault in Our Stars in 2012. When did you realize: “Wow, I have really hit something new here ?” I remember I was on the road for about a month touring. I got home, and I called my agent and I said: “When does this end?”

And she said: “You don’t really choose.” How did you feel in that moment?

Both excited and trapped, which I think is the nature of celebrity a little bit – that it’s exciting and also claustrophobic. You have a choice about how public to make your life. You don’t really have a choice about the public’s response to that.

On the other hand, it was wonderful to have the book reaching so many millions of people. Living with all that at the same time was both exciting and challenging, like it is for the young people in Hollywood, Ending.

It’s much harder for them because I was 35 years old and married and had kids and the foundational relationships in my life were pretty set. When this happens when you’re 22, as it happens to a lot of people, whether they’re influencers or actors, you often don’t have those relationships. It can be really disorienting.

It sounds to me like you’re saying: “This thing that was happening around my house, around my family, that was more real. ” Why did the excitement around the book feel unreal?

I don’t think it ever feels real, to be honest with you. I think it always feels like that’s happening to someone else. One of the things that [Andy] Warhol saw coming is that people don’t really see famous people as people. They see them as both more than people and less than people. They objectify them in every imaginable way. They feel free to comment on their bodies, they feel free to comment on their work as if they weren’t people, and so on.

The other thing is that I wanted really badly to be successful. I think I wanted much more than would be healthy to be successful. I had no concept of what it would actually feel like. It was really rewarding to have so many people respond to the books and the story so generously. But the fame part of fame was quite empty.

I don’t think I was liked very much in middle school. I really struggled with making friends. I thought that if I was famous, then everyone would be my friend and like me. That turns out to be a little bit of an oversimplification.

A lot of people don’t like you, right? The nature of being famous is that everybody has an opinion about you, but not everybody has a positive opinion about you. That’s one thing that I hadn’t really thought very hard about.

The other thing is that compliments simply don’t penetrate. I believe people in the abstract when they say that my work has been helpful to them or that it has been meaningful for them, and I’m extremely grateful for that. I don’t want to disbelieve them because that would dishonor the gift that they’ve given me by investing in my work and by bringing their deepest selves to it.

But the criticism just penetrates in a different way. I believe it, because deep down there’s something about me that believes I don’t deserve any of this and I’m an impostor and I’m not a very good writer.

You and your brother Hank have been creating videos for YouTube since 2007. How do you feel about your legacy as a pioneer of the social internet?

Hank and I try really hard to do interesting, useful, fun, meaningful stuff in online spaces that build community and also make the world suck less. I hope that we’ve been able to do some of that. But there’s no question that just participating in an algorithmically generated internet is morally complex.

You’re competing with Mr Beast for clicks. Even if I’m making an educational video that’s intended for high school students to be able to understand US history or physics or organic chemistry or whatever, I’m still competing for clicks with people who will do or say literally anything for clicks.

Do you think, feeling the way you feel now about the social internet, you would have started making YouTube videos if you had to do it all over again?

I’d do it again because it’s been an amazing experience and it’s been such a gift in my life.

I might do it without my face in the videos, to be honest with you. That’s the big difference. A lot of my educational video friends don’t have their faces in their videos, and I find that admirable.

But so much of the community you build is, frankly, parasocial. Yeah, it is. It is face-based. It’s hard to imagine not doing it that way.

Actually, the time when Hank and I both realized that we weren’t actually in control of what we share was when Hank got cancer a couple years ago. We realized one of two things was gonna happen.

One: Hank was going to, for the first time in 20 years, take eight months away from making Vlogbrothers videos without an explanation. Or, two: he was going to be forced to talk about having cancer in public.

Hank ended up dealing with it beautifully by not just talking about having cancer, but by sort of science-communicating his way through cancer treatment, which is a very Hank Green thing to do.

What do you make of the fact that in the age of the social internet, so many people, particularly young people, really just wanna be famous? The fame itself is a goal.

Not only is the fame itself a goal, fame has become so decoupled from wealth that no longer is fame a guarantee of financial security. I have a friend, for example, who was a famous TikToker and also worked at the Gap. People would come to the Gap where they worked and be like: “Why are you working?” They would be like: “For money. Because this is where I work.”

I suspect that young people want to be famous for the same reason I wanted public attention, which is that I thought it would fill a hole inside of me. What fills the hole is real connection, which is the relationships that are gonna sustain you through everything you have to survive.

It’s interesting that you’re saying this. In an interview you did last year with the New York Times , you talked about feeling like people believe the internet fills a hole – but then, you didn’t really want to tell young people not to try to use the internet to heal themselves. I’m wondering if you have different advice for young people now.

It’s so hard. I’m going through this now with one of my godchildren, where when you don’t have the relationships that you want to have in your community because you’re different – as I was – or because your interests are too niche or whatever it is, you find connection online. I was part of the first generation of people who found that, in 1993 on CompuServe. It was revelatory, to be able to not be stuck inside of a body that was frail and embarrassing and full of failure, and instead to be this creature online where I could really connect with people. Some of the people I connected with, I’m still connected to. I’m so grateful for that.

Yet at the same time, it can’t replace what we experience with real life connection. I do feel a little differently than I did a year or two ago. I do think we have to build meaningful relationships with each other in meat space, as they say online.

I think it’s very helpful to be reminded that my body is made out of meat, that even the thinking parts are made out of meat. It’s very easy online to lose track of the fact that you’re a mammal. You’re much, much, much closer to being a squirrel than you are to being an artificial intelligence.

I feel like in the book and in this conversation, you are suggesting that fame is corrosive to us and that the online attention economy is not good for us. But having a social media platform, having a personal brand, being on camera – that is all stuff that more and more people just have to engage with, not in order to necessarily be famous, but to have a professional life . How are we supposed to move forward?

What the book concludes, I hope, is that we have to seize the reins of power and understand that we have more power than we think we have as internet citizens, as creators online.

I remember suddenly becoming conscious on the set of The Fault in Our Stars that everyone cared what I thought. The reason they cared what I thought was not because I’m an incredibly compelling person, but because I had millions of followers on Twitter and at any moment I could blow up the movie. Understanding that with the sacrifices involved in participating in the social internet – there is also an exchange of power. Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk don’t have all the power, as evidenced by the declining role of X in society. They have a lot of power. They have too much power. Way, way, way too much power. But, combined, we have more.

Hollywood, Ending is to some extent about how much you have to feed the content beasts in order to succeed. So I did want to ask about a recent dust-up that Hank was involved in, where he was accused of using AI to write part of a script for a video. He addressed the controversy. He said that AI did not write the script but admitted to relying on AI more and more to research his work. That’s honestly understandable to me, because he really produces a lot. Hank suggested that you and he had spoken and that you had some criticism of his AI use. Are you comfortable telling me about those criticisms?

Yeah, it’s more than being critical of his AI use in particular. I have my own opinions. I don’t use LLMs and don’t see a need to use them in my work.

It was more about the fact of what you just said, which is Hank makes a lot of stuff. I think especially in the last couple of years, Hank has been obsessively trying to get everything in his head out into the world and I think that is not healthy. We’ve had that conversation and that’s part of being a brother. Hank’s had those conversations with me many times before.

Trying to get everything out of your head seems like a pretty reasonable response to a bad health scare.

Yeah, I think it is a reasonable response to mortality. I think the more reasonable response – not that I’m here to lecture my brother – is to invest in your core relationships.

You have expressed mixed feelings about people seeing too much of you in the art you make. I have spent this interview very much reading you into Hollywood, Ending. How do you feel about that?

You haven’t read into it in a way that makes me uncomfortable, so I feel fine about it. There are other things you could have read into it that would have bothered me.

It’s uncomfortable to be read into the book because I don’t want to be a character in the book. I have written two nonfiction books now and six novels, and writing fiction is so much more vulnerable and intimate than writing nonfiction.

It just is. Because I have to go to deeper places within me. I have to go to places that nobody else knows about, not even the people closest to me. That’s really hard work, but it’s good work because I’m asking the reader to do the same. I’m asking them to bring their deepest selves to the story, to bring their own particular traumas and fears and loves and losses to the story in a way that no one else can. That’s asking a lot. So I have to do the work on the other side to make that worth it. Hopefully.
paragraphs: Returning with his first-ever adult novel, the bestselling author reflects on fame, YouTube and his brother’s AI controversy

By his mid-30s, John Green had done pretty well for himself. His debut novel, Looking for Alaska, had won a prestigious award for young adult literature. He and his brother, Hank, had launched a popular YouTube channel, where they regularly posted videos about their lives. With their combined incomes, Green and his wife were able to cobble together a living, buying a house and starting a family in Indianapolis.

“The week that book came out, it sold more copies than all of my previous books had sold in hardcover combined,” Green recalled in a recent interview with the Guardian podcast Stateside with Kai and Carter . “Up until that moment, I’d been very cavalier about sharing my life online and offline, and it was only in the wake of that that I started to realize the cost of that. People started coming to our house, sometimes quite late at night. We had young kids – babies – back then. People don’t always have the best boundaries.”

The Fault in Our Stars follows the story of Hazel, a 16-year-old living with cancer, who falls in love with a fellow cancer patient. Powered in part by Green’s online fandom, the book sold more than 20m copies – enough for every person in the state of New York to have a copy, and then some. In 2014, Hollywood adapted it into a movie starring Shailene Woodley and Ansel Elgort. After the film became a blockbuster, raking in more than $300m at the global box office, Hollywood started adapting Green’s other books, too.
But he remains decidedly ambivalent about his popularity. It doesn’t feel nourishing, he said. It feels like empty calories.

“It was uncomfortable to talk about, because how do you not be grateful for this overwhelmingly wonderful thing in your life?” Green said. “I have a friend who’s a very successful author, and I remember she said to me once: ‘Of all the good things that ever happened to me, fame was the worst.’ I think that’s a pretty good way to think about it.”

Green decided to work through his mixed feelings in his new book, Hollywood, Ending. Released this week, the book follows two young actors who make a movie about Andy Warhol, fall in love, and try to stay sane as they sell pieces of themselves to the internet and the Hollywood publicity machine. It’s Green’s first novel in nearly a decade, and his first-ever for adults. But it still feels like a classic John Green book – thanks, predominantly, to its ardent belief that art, and other people, can help us survive anything. In an era in which more and more people must market themselves on social media, courting the dizzying highs and crushing lows of fame, Green still hopes we’ll find something better.
I spoke with Green about the moral complexity of the attention economy, what he wishes he had done differently as a pioneering YouTuber and his brother Hank’s recent AI controversy.
